decisions.comment: Hybrid Canvas with Workbench project/file viewer; commands in context menus/Ctrl+K/drag-pin; UE5-style pin shape/color semantics; types hover-only; compact getter capsules; embeddable variables; graphite streamlined UI.

decisions.title: jetos Studio — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: Which experience Studio is built around — settings app, review-first changesets, ops board, or an editable source document.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — the document is the app, the rail finds things, the health strip watches the fleet, and nothing lands without the changeset review. Every edit path — widget, alert fix, rollback — funnels through one gate.
decisions.story: Nate wants to bump halcyon's kernel and flip a theme option; later that week a bad generation fails to boot and he needs rollback fast. Four genuinely different apps answer those moments: find-and-flip settings, stage-review-apply changesets, a fleet health board, or config.jet itself rendered as a live document. All four share one visual system and the same truth — every GUI edit rewrites exactly one system.jet line and shows the diff (the real set-option transaction). Browse side by side: file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#studio (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
// config.jet (halcyon fixture) — the source every archetype edits
boot.kernel: .CachyOS
boot.loader: .Limine
perf.scheduler: .ScxLavd
desktop.plasma.enable: true
theme.flavor: "catppuccin-mocha"
secrets.wifi: age("wifi.age")
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid Studio, but replace the projectional-document foundation with a normal clean dashboard + sidebar app. Landing page is a simple opsboard-style dashboard: hosts, health, services, generations, alerts, and monitoring status are easy to understand at a glance. Settings live in sidebar categories, with an extensible category/page registry so future Studio modules can add sections without redesign. Changeset is a first-class sidebar page/category for comparing diffs, impact, and generation changes. Settings and monitoring belong in appropriate sidebar categories. Keep the hybrid one-apply-path rule: edits from settings, alerts, rollback, or changeset review stage into the same changeset/apply gate. Visual style follows the cleaner Settings option; information structure follows Ops board where useful. Do not build the projectional config document as the primary UI right now.

options.name: Settings — find it, flip it, apply
options.detail:
Core loop: pick a category, flip one option's control, confirm the single source line it writes, apply. Apple-System-Settings navigator whose sidebar groups map 1:1 to config.jet namespaces; the signature is the pending source tray — a docked bar accumulating the exact +/- lines and impact chips as you toggle, so nothing touches the machine unseen. Kernel change: Boot & kernel → dropdown (tagged rebuild+reboot). Rollback: Generations category → "Roll back to N". The beginner tier: lowest ceremony for changing one thing. options.name: Changeset — review before anything lands
options.detail:
Core loop: stage edits from anywhere into one changeset whose primary screen is the diff review plus impact, then apply the whole reviewed set as one build. The GitHub-PR/terraform-plan model: unified source diff with per-hunk include/exclude, beside a plain-language "What this changes" summary and an impact ledger (services restarted, packages rebuilt, reboot needed, generation N+1). Build & switch = merge. Rollback stages the inverse as a reviewable changeset. The safety tier: never surprised by an apply. Risk: heavier for a one-toggle change; authoring via option-key form assumes some fluency (autocomplete helps).

options.name: Ops board — health first, edit on drill-in
options.detail:
Core loop: watch the fleet health board; when a tile goes red, drill into it, fix or roll back from the drawer, watch it go green. Landing screen is KPIs, alerts, per-host generation ribbons (colored run history), and a service grid — the Proxmox/Tailscale/PagerDuty model. Config editing is a drawer opened FROM a red thing; the mock's centerpiece is a kernel panic on gen 42 with auto-fallback to 41 and one-click clean rollback, the diagnosis in what/why/fix voice. Hosts come from workspace.jet. The fleet tier: operate constantly, edit rarely. Risk: drawer editing is intentionally shallow — deep edits should deep-link into A or D.

options.name: Projectional — the file is the app
options.detail:
Core loop: read the config AS the document; edit each value through an inline control so you change system.jet without typing syntax. config.jet rendered line-numbered and syntax-highlighted, but every option value is a live widget in place — toggle, dropdown, stepper, chip list, sealed secret. A Text toggle reveals the exact source the projection produces (one artifact, two surfaces); a git-style gutter marks changed lines; the generation picker turns the document into a time machine ("Restore these values" stages a rollback). The JetBrains-MPS/Dark model — the expert tier, I8-clean (same set-option mechanism, different entrypoint). Risk: real implementation must round-trip through the formatter; densest for beginners.

Core loop: land on the fleet health strip; read config.jet as a live document the category rail navigates; every widget edit stages into one changeset; open the tray to review the diff + impact, then build — a red alert and a past generation both funnel back through that same changeset. Takes: projectional foundation (inline widgets, git-gutter, Text mirror, generation time-machine) + settings' rail as navigation INTO the document (no separate detail pane — the doc is the detail) + changeset as the only apply path (persistent tray → review sheet: plain summary, impact ledger, per-hunk diff, Build only / Build & switch; rollback stages the inverse) + opsboard's landing strip (hosts, generation ribbons, alerts; a red alert deep-links to the offending option with what/why/fix). decisions.title: Core process spawning and pipeline surface
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical subprocess API beyond one-shot process.run.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A gives beginners the safe argv-only one-shot they already have, and gives experts a typed ProcessSpec/Child handle for streaming, timeouts, env/cwd, signals, pipelines, and output limits. One semantic mechanism: process.run is sugar over ProcessSpec.run.
decisions.story: Nora writes a Jet build tool. It must run a compiler, stream logs live, kill it after 30 seconds, pass a clean environment, pipe generated code into a formatter, and preserve the child's exact exit status. A capture-everything process.run either hangs, hides progress, or forces her into shell strings.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: a fluent builder can become opaque magic; raw spawn knobs can become a shell footgun. Patch: argv lists only by default, no shell interpolation helper in Core, every knob is a typed field on ProcessSpec, and shell execution remains an explicit expert escape if ever approved separately.

options.name: ProcessSpec + Child handles (recommended)
options.detail: Keep process.run(argv) as beginner sugar. Add process.cmd(argv) -> ProcessSpec with cwd/env/stdin/stdout/stderr/timeout/output_limit methods, spawn() -> Child, wait()/kill()/terminate()/interrupt(), typed ExitStatus, streaming readers/writers, and process.pipeline([...]) for argv-only pipelines without a shell.
options.code:
use core.process as process
use core.time as time

spec :: process.cmd(["cargo", "test"])
    .cwd("crates/app")
    .env_clear()
    .env("RUST_BACKTRACE", "1")
    .stdout(.Stream)
    .stderr(.Inherit)
    .timeout(time.seconds(30))

child :: spec.spawn()?
loop line in child.stdout.lines() { print(line) }
status :: child.wait()?
if !status.success { process.exit(status.code ?? 1) }

pipe :: process.pipeline([
    process.cmd(["cat", "input.txt"]),
    process.cmd(["grep", "error"]),
])?

options.name: Many direct module functions
options.detail: Add process.run_stream, run_timeout, run_env, pipeline, kill, etc. Discoverable in autocomplete, but the surface becomes a pile of near-duplicates and option combinations explode.
options.code:
process.run_timeout(["cargo", "test"], time.seconds(30))?
process.run_env(["env"], ["A=1"])?
process.pipeline([["cat", "x"], ["grep", "y"]])?

options.name: Shell string convenience
options.detail: Expose process.shell("cargo test 2>&1 | tee log") as the powerful path. Familiar for experts, but it makes injection and quoting footguns the blessed default unless gated separately.
options.code: process.shell("cd crates/app && cargo test 2>&1 | tee log")?

options.name: Keep one-shot run only
options.detail: Document that serious process orchestration should use external tools. This keeps Jet worse than Python subprocess, Go os/exec, and Rust std::process for build tools and agent operations.
options.code:
r :: process.run(["cargo", "test"])?
print(r.output)

comparisons.note: subprocess.run/Popen is flexible but easy to misuse with shell=True and text/bytes confusion. Jet can keep argv-only defaults and typed streams.
exec.Command gives explicit argv/cwd/env/stdout fields; pipelines require manual pipe wiring. Jet can wrap that pattern in a typed ProcessSpec and pipeline helper.
std::process::Command is the right safety shape, but verbose for common streaming and timeout cases. Jet can keep the shape and improve ergonomics.

decisions.title: jet dev server — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: Where the dev server's richness lives: in the browser, in the terminal, or mirrored identically in both.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — parity keeps both surfaces honest for free (one poll, one vocabulary), and each side gets its native depth on demand: the full overlay in the browser, the request log in the terminal. No starved surface, no second source of truth.
decisions.story: Kai runs `jet dev app.jet --target=web` with the browser on one monitor and the terminal on the other. On a broken save the last good build keeps serving — but where does he learn what broke, and how much does each surface tell him? Three splits of the same information: rich browser + silent terminal, rich terminal + clean browser, or strict parity where both always show the same status and the same verbatim E0102 frame. Browse: file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#devserver (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet --target=web
serving http://localhost:8080 — watching app.jet …
# save a typo → E0102. Last good build keeps serving;
# the archetype decides where the error reaches Kai.
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid dev server, with the nicely formatted terminal dashboard header pinned. The header remains visible while request logs, rebuild output, verbose detail, and errors scroll below. Keep mirrored browser status/overlay and terminal depth, but the pinned dashboard header is required as the terminal anchor.

options.name: Quiet terminal, rich browser
options.detail:
Core loop: live in the browser; the terminal is a three-line daemon. Terminal prints URL, watch target, last rebuild — then goes silent. Everything rich is in the page: vite-class full error overlay with the verbatim diagnostic, dim-while-rebuilding, a rebuild toast with timing, reconnect states. Matches how web developers actually work — eyes on the rendered page. Risk: with no tab open an error is invisible until you look (the terminal still prints the diagnostic as fallback).
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/quiet.html
options.code:
terminal (steady state)          browser (on error)
 ┌───────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────────────┐
 │ jet dev  serving      │   │ localhost:8080                 │
 │   :8080               │   │ ┌ Build failed ────── app.jet ┐│
 │   watching app.jet    │   │ │ Error [E0102]: nothing named ││
 │ ✓ rebuilt 0.4s 14:22  │   │ │  `nonexistent_function_xyz`… ││
 └───────────────────────┘   │ │  8 | nonexistent_function()  ││
                             │ │    | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^  ││
  toast: ● rebuilt in 0.4s   │ │ Why / Fix … · Esc dismiss    ││
                             │ └──────────────────────────────┘│
                             └────────────────────────────────┘

options.name: Terminal dashboard, clean browser
options.detail:
Core loop: the terminal is the primary view — a pinned header (status dot, port, client count, last build time) over a scrolling request/rebuild log with timings; the browser shows only a thin error banner pointing back. Best for terminal-centric developers and multi-client debugging: every request and rebuild visible with timing, client count comes free from the 400ms pollers. Risk: pinned header needs cursor-home redraw (std ANSI) and degrades to a plain status line off-TTY; the browser is deliberately information-poor.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/dashboard.html
options.code:
┌ jet dev ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ ● ready   localhost:8080   2 clients   last build 0.4s│
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  14:22:03  GET  /            200  2ms
  14:22:07  save app.jet  →  rebuilt 0.4s
  14:23:01  save app.jet  →  error E0102
  Error [E0102]: nothing named `nonexistent_function_xyz` …
    8 | nonexistent_function_xyz()
      | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

 browser: ● Build failed · E0102 — details in the terminal

options.name: Paired — same truth on both sides
options.detail:
Core loop: glance at the terminal or the browser corner — same status, same error. A one-line terminal status and a browser corner strip mirror each other exactly (building / ok / error / n clients), both driven by the same version poll; on error both expand the identical verbatim diagnostic frame (once in ANSI, once in CSS, same snapshot text). No "which surface is authoritative" question, lowest cognitive overhead. Risk: parity must be genuinely lockstep or it's a lie; the frame is the only detail level — no request log.
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/paired.html

options.name: Hybrid — mirrored status with on-demand depth
options.detail:
Core loop: a one-line terminal status and a browser corner strip mirror the same poll; on error the browser strip expands to the full overlay and the terminal can expand to a request log, but the parity line is always the shared truth. Takes: paired's contract (identical state from one poll — they cannot drift) + quiet's full vite-class overlay as the strip's expanded state (room, not a second truth) + dashboard's request/rebuild log behind v/--verbose, printed under the same parity header. Left out: any deliberately starved surface — no mute-daemon terminal, no info-poor browser banner; depth is additive on both sides of one status mechanism (I8).
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/devserver/hybrid.html
options.code:
terminal (parity line)            browser (strip = collapsed overlay)

                                   │  (app)     ● ready · 2 cl  │
                                   └────────────────────────────┘

 ┌ E0102 ─────────────────────┐    │  (app, dimmed)             │
 │ Error [E0102]: nothing      │    │ ┌ Build failed ── app.jet ┐│
 │   named `nonexistent_...`   │    │ │ Error [E0102]: nothing  ││

decisions.title: Canvas node states: how a disabled node and a debug-only node are spelled in source
decisions.gist: What Jet source looks like when a Canvas node is switched off temporarily, and how a node can be marked to exist only in debug builds.
decisions.explainer: One attribute family gives both Blueprint states with real syntax that survives fmt/refactors and stays type-checked (a comment marker silently rots when the code around it is renamed); #DebugOnly hides the comptime plumbing beginners should never need to see, while comptime if build.profile remains available to experts if C's value is also ratified later.
decisions.story: Priya is wiring a pricing function in Canvas. A logging call keeps cluttering her test output, so she wants to switch that node off for a while without deleting it — same as unplugging a cable, not cutting it. Separately, she has a sanity-check node that should run in dev builds but must never ship in the release binary. Canvas is source-backed: both states must be spelled in the .jet file somehow, and today Jet has no spelling for either (only build.os exists as a comptime value, no debug/release distinction).

options.name: Comment marker for off, no debug-only yet
options.detail: Disabled node = the statement commented out with a marker comment Canvas recognizes and can re-enable. Zero new language surface; code is genuinely inert because it is a comment. Debug-only nodes wait for a separate build-profile decision.

options.name: #Off attribute statement gate
options.detail: A real attribute the compiler parses and skips (still type-checked, like Rust's #[cfg] siblings or C#'s [Conditional]). Survives formatting and refactors as real syntax; Canvas toggles it. Debug-only becomes #Off("release") or a sibling attribute later.

options.name: build.profile comptime value + comptime if (debug-only), comment marker (off)
options.detail: Adds build.profile (.Debug | .Release) beside build.os; debug-only nodes project as a comptime if rail Canvas renders as a badge, folded at compile time exactly like build.os dispatch. Temporary off stays the A-style comment marker since 'off' is a workspace state, not a program state.

options.name: Both as attributes: #Off and #DebugOnly
options.detail: One attribute family for node states: #Off (skipped every build, still type-checked) and #DebugOnly (compiled only when the build profile is debug; requires the same build-profile machinery as C under the hood but the user never sees comptime if).

comparisons.note: Nodes have a Disabled state (greyed, skipped) and a Development Only mode (hazard-striped, compiled out of shipping builds) — the two states Priya expects.
comparisons.code: Right-click node -> Disable Node / Development Only

comparisons.note: cfg attributes gate code by build profile; debug_assert! is the idiomatic debug-only check that vanishes in release.
[Conditional("DEBUG")] methods compile to nothing in release while the call sites stay type-checked.
comparisons.code:
[Conditional("DEBUG")]
static void AssertBalanced(Cart c, decimal t) { ... }

decisions.title: jetos is a from-scratch standalone OS; NixOS module system is not a backend
decisions.gist: jetos must be its own Linux system — jet, jetpack, and the hangar all the way down — functionally equivalent to NixOS. Building it by generating a NixOS configuration under the hood produces a reskinned NixOS and is forbidden.
decisions.story: The first working graphical jetos VM was realized by compiling the jetos option tree into a generated NixOS flake. It booted GNOME, but the guest was visibly NixOS: NixOS wallpaper, release codename "Yarara", NixOS module semantics throughout. The owner rejected this outright: adapters may leverage the nixpkgs package ecosystem, but the operating system itself — module/option system, generations, activation, /etc rendering, service units, boot, desktop glue, identity — must be jetos-native.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os vm run halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
boots a system whose settings panel reads "jetos" because it IS jetos: hangar store, jetos-generated systemd units, jetos activation — with firefox/steam/plasma fetched from nixpkgs through the jetpack adapter.

options.label: Native jetos system, nixpkgs as package adapter only
options.detail: jetos owns every OS-assembly concern natively; nixpkgs is reached through jetpack providers purely to obtain packages. Functional equivalence to NixOS is proven by behavior, not by sharing its implementation.

options.label: Hidden NixOS realizer (rejected)
options.detail: Compile jetos config to a generated NixOS system, rebrand the output. Fast to ship, but the product is a NixOS fork/reskin.

decisions.comment: Decreed live 2026-07-09: no forked/reskinned NixOS; standalone jetos with nixpkgs adapters.

decisions.title: On-disk package store inside a jetos system: hangar-native, staged
decisions.gist: The jetpack hangar is THE store of a jetos system — its layout, GC, and generation roots. Stage 1 keeps nixpkgs-built closures under a hangar-managed compatibility root so unmodified binaries run; a later stage re-roots/rebuilds packages natively.
decisions.story: Nixpkgs binaries hardcode /nix/store paths internally (ELF interpreters, dlopen paths, wrappers). Running them unmodified requires that path shape to exist on disk. Rather than adopting /nix/store as jetos's permanent format, the hangar owns the store from day one and treats the nix-shaped subtree as the adapter's compatibility root, with native re-rooting as the planned end state.
decisions.inWild:
/hangar/…            ← jetos store: metadata, GC roots, generations
/hangar/compat/nix/store/…   ← stage-1 root for unmodified nixpkgs closures
Later: packages rebuilt against hangar paths; compat root shrinks to nothing.

options.label: Hangar-native, staged compat root
options.detail: Hangar owns everything; nix-shaped compat subtree is an adapter detail with a planned exit.

options.label: Keep /nix/store layout permanently
options.detail: Simplest compatibility, least ownership of the format.

options.label: Hangar-native from day one
options.detail: Rewrite/rebuild every package before anything ships; purest but gates all system work.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09.

decisions.title: No `nix` binary anywhere in the jetos product path — this epoch builds jetpack's own nixpkgs pipeline
decisions.gist: jetos and jetpack must not shell out to the nix binary. Leveraging the nixpkgs ecosystem requires jetpack to evaluate, fetch, and build nixpkgs packages itself: a Nix-language evaluator (or equivalent artifact protocol), derivation hashing, the binary-cache substituter protocol, and a sandboxed builder — in scope for this epoch, not deferred.
decisions.story: Today the jetpack nix provider runs `nix build nixpkgs#pkg`. That makes the nix binary a load-bearing dependency of every jetos system build. The owner chose the strongest form of independence: the adapter speaks nixpkgs' formats (Nix language, drv hashing, NAR/narinfo caches) through jetpack's own implementation, so no Nix-project executable is required to build or run a jetos system.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack fetch nixpkgs#firefox
  evaluates nixpkgs with jetpack's evaluator, resolves the store hash,
  substitutes the NAR from cache.nixos.org into the hangar compat root —
  no /run/current-system/sw/bin/nix involved.

options.label: Staged: nix CLI now, native later
options.detail: Ship on the CLI, replace it on a scoped later card.

options.label: nix CLI permanently acceptable
options.detail: Never build an evaluator.

options.label: No nix binary at all this epoch
options.detail: The epoch includes jetpack's own evaluation/fetch/build pipeline before jetos ships.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09: no nix binary at all this epoch.

decisions.title: Epoch-7 exit bar: NixOS-class architecture natively + prioritized breadth
decisions.gist: The epoch exits when jetos natively delivers the full NixOS capability architecture (typed module/option system, generations, atomic activation, rollback, fully declarative system) PLUS: a terminal baseline, a graphical baseline, one-line desktop swaps (GNOME/KDE/Hyprland/niri; wayland/x11), and the owner's entire ~/nixos config running natively. Module breadth beyond that grows by demand through a defined process.
decisions.story: NixOS has on the order of 20k options; literal total parity is a multi-year tail. Functional equivalence is an architecture property plus enough module breadth to cover real systems. Nothing is baked into jetos itself: the entire system is driven by the user's jet config files — defaults may exist (terminal and graphical baselines), but composition is wholly the user's, written by hand or through jetos Studio.
decisions.inWild:
desktop: .Gnome        →  desktop: .Kde        (one line)
session: .Wayland      →  session: .X11        (one line)
desktop: .Hyprland — same config file, nothing else changes.

options.label: Architecture + prioritized breadth
options.detail: Exit = architecture + baselines + one-line desktop swaps + owner config native; breadth by demand after.

options.label: Full module parity
options.detail: Every NixOS option has a jetos equivalent before exit.

options.label: Owner config only
options.detail: Exit = owner's machine runs; everything else later.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09.

decisions.title: Fate of the jet→NixOS realizer: demoted to a clearly-labeled migration tool
decisions.gist: The generated-NixOS build path (formerly the `--real` tier realizer, D-JOS-NIXBACKEND1) is never a product path. It survives only as an explicit, clearly-labeled migration/transition tool for A/B-ing a config during a NixOS→jetos migration. The nixos→jet importer remains central and unaffected.
decisions.story: The realizer exists and works — it built and booted a rebranded NixOS from a jet config. Under D-JOS-NATIVE1 that can never ship as jetos. Its remaining value is migration: while a user transitions, building their jet config both ways and comparing behavior gives confidence the conversion is faithful.

$ jet os migrate compare halcyon
  builds the config natively (jetos) and via the NixOS oracle, boots both,
  diffs services/packages/session facts — labeled a migration aid, not jetos.

options.label: Delete entirely
options.detail: Parity verified against a plain NixOS guest built from the user's real flake instead.

options.label: Keep as labeled migration tool
options.detail: Exposed as an explicit transition command, separate from the native build path.

decisions.title: Derive output: emit Jet source via $ splice, re-parsed and sema-checked?
decisions.gist: User-authored derives need a way to emit code. D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratifies that output must re-enter lexer/parser/sema (never bypass it). This decision fixes the surface: the `$` splice inside `comptime { }` is the output mechanism. Opens only if D-USERDERIVE1 passes.
decisions.explainer: D-CTCODEGEN1 forbids derives from emitting Rust directly or manipulating the AST in-place — all output must be Jet source that re-enters the front end. The `$` splice already exists for comptime value injection. The question is whether derive output is the same `$` splice mechanism (extended to emit function/impl blocks) or a separate API (typed AST builder). A typed AST builder is a second mechanism for emitting code — I8 violation. The `$` splice path means all derive errors appear in Jet source terms, not in opaque AST operations (I2/I3 compliant). The main risk is that splicing multi-line impl blocks requires the splice to carry statement-level fragments, not just expressions — a small extension to the existing mechanic.
decisions.story: My derive_Serialize function builds up a String of Jet source for the encode/decode methods, then splices it in with `${ ... }`. The parser re-reads it; sema checks the types; if I made a mistake, the error points at the generated Jet, not at rustc output.

options.name: $ splice emits Jet source fragments, re-parsed and sema-checked
options.detail: Extend the existing `$` splice to carry statement- and item-level Jet source (not just expressions). The emitted text re-enters the lexer and parser exactly as user-written Jet would. Sema sees the expanded code; errors appear in Jet source terms. One mechanism for comptime output; I8 satisfied; I2/I3 satisfied.

options.name: Typed AST builder API
options.detail: Derives call a builder API (`ImplBlock.new()`, `.add_method()`, etc.) that constructs a typed AST node directly. No string parsing; type-safe at the builder call sites. A second mechanism for emitting code alongside the `$` splice — I8 tension. Builder API surface must be designed, stabilized, and versioned separately.

options.name: Defer derive output mechanism
options.detail: Approve D-USERDERIVE1 and D-METAREFLECT1 but leave the output mechanism open. Reflection ships; derives cannot emit code yet. Partial; blocks the actual derive use cases; not a useful intermediate state.

comparisons.note: Rust proc-macros receive and emit `TokenStream` — effectively source text in token form, re-parsed by the compiler. The `quote!` macro is the ergonomic surface. Jet's `$` splice is the same concept with Jet syntax.
Zig comptime functions return types directly — a typed approach closer to option B. No string emission; the comptime function is the mechanism. Works because Zig's type system is the API surface.

decisions.title: jetpack / jetos CLI output — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: How command progress and results are experienced: a scrolling ledger, a pinned live region, or plan→confirm→apply.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — one output model whose depth is decided by consequence, not by command: quiet where the stakes are low, a live region where the wait is long, a plan gate where the machine changes. The tier rule must be stated policy, not a guess.
decisions.story: Leo runs `jetpack add`, `jet env`, `jetos switch`, and the occasional `jetpack gc`. The flows are identical in all three options — what differs is the experience of progress and consequence: read a quiet ledger top to bottom, watch one live region while clean scrollback accumulates above it, or review a complete plan and answer once before anything mutates (the nh/terraform model you named). One shared theme; diagnostics verbatim (E0102). Browse: file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#cli (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
$ jetos switch
# 42 → 43: kernel bump, one add, one remove.
# The archetype decides what Leo sees between typing this
# and the new generation being live — and when he gets to say no.
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid CLI. Keep colored + / - / ~ plan symbols. Both -y and --yes must bypass the confirmation gate consistently. Add nh-style dependency chain/graph visualization where appropriate during long download/build/realization phases: show downloads, builds, dependencies, and current edge/progress in the pinned live region/apply progress. Scrollback remains the ledger; non-TTY/NO_COLOR degrades to deterministic plain text.

options.name: Ledger — quiet scrolling record
options.detail:
Core loop: read top to bottom once; the active line spins, done lines freeze, scrollback is the permanent record. Refines what jetpack already ships (gutter, ✓ rows, threshold rule, spinner) — zero learning cost, perfect log fidelity, identical on TTY and CI. Cost: a long op is a wall of lines and there's no single "where am I now"; the spinner line is the only live signal.

options.name: Live region — one place to watch
options.detail:
Core loop: watch one pinned bottom region (progress bar, counts, elapsed, size); finished items promote up into clean scrollback; the region collapses to a one-line summary. The uv/bun/pnpm model — best "where am I now" for long builds: one aggregate 31/42 beats 42 log lines. Cost: cursor-up region redraw (std ANSI, noted in NOTES), must erase cleanly before any diagnostic prints, and non-TTY degrades to appended lines (= option A).

  realizing 1/2 · fd            00:06 · 42 MB
  ████████████████░░░░░░░░  unpacking
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        │ finished items promote UP, region stays pinned
        ▼
  jetpack  2 packages ready in 6s  ✓   (region replaced)

options.name: Plan — decide first, apply quietly
options.detail:
Core loop: every mutation prints a full plan (add/change/remove, download size, closure and generation delta), asks once [y/N], then applies tersely with each done line tied to a plan line. The nh/terraform model — safest for consequential ops (switch, gc): you decide from the diff and nothing mutates unseen. Cost: an extra step on trivial adds — needs sensible --yes and CI behavior (non-TTY prints the plan and exits without applying, never hangs).

    ~ linux         6.9.7  → 6.10.1
    - obsolete-lib  1.2.0  → —

  Download 240 MB · closure +18 MB · rebuild boot + current

  Apply? [y/N] ▏

     Enter/N → nothing touched

options.name: Hybrid — consequence-scaled output
options.detail:
Core loop: output scales with consequence — trivial ops print a quiet ledger, long builds pin a live region that promotes finished lines into that ledger, and mutations gate on a plan first; the scrollback is always the record. Takes: ledger as the spine under everything + live's region for genuinely long work (finished items promote up as permanent ledger lines, region collapses to a summary) + plan's gate for mutations only (jetos switch, gc), whose apply reuses the same region-into-ledger flow with each ✓ tied to a plan line. Left out: plan's gate on trivial adds (prompt fatigue; --yes still available) and a region for short ops. One progress experience at three depths, chosen by what the command does (I8). Non-TTY: no region, mutation prints plan and exits.

decisions.title: Add a full logic-programming subset (backtracking, multi-answer relations) to Jet?
decisions.gist: Research notes caution against a full logic-programming subset. The gentler slice — failure-aware iterators and comprehensions — is already on the roadmap. The question is whether to add true multi-answer relations and backtracking on top of that, or hold the line.
decisions.explainer: Full LP (Prolog-style) requires unification, a choice-point stack, and a non-deterministic execution model that cuts across Jet's deterministic ownership semantics. It would introduce a second execution model with different rules for variable binding, mutation, and resource cleanup — directly conflicting with I8 and with the safety-by-default guarantee. The failure-aware-comprehension card covers the practical 90% case (generators that can fail or produce multiple results) without a separate execution model. A full LP subsystem would also complicate the JIT tier and codegen.
decisions.story: I want to write a solver that enumerates valid configurations of a constraint system — like a puzzle solver or a type-inference engine — without shelling out to Prolog.

options.name: Reject full LP — keep failure-aware iterators only
options.detail: The failure-aware-comprehension card already targets the practical use cases. Full backtracking introduces a second execution model (choice points, unification) incompatible with deterministic ownership. Recommend keeping the door closed.

options.name: Adopt a scoped LP subset (relations block)
options.detail: A `@logic { }` block opts in to a Datalog-style subset: finite relations, no function symbols, stratified negation. Bounded and terminating, so no infinite search trees. Still a second execution model — variables inside the block bind differently — which violates I8.

options.name: Far-horizon: post-v1 constraint/solver research
options.detail: Park LP as a research item. A future constraint-programming library (not a language feature) could implement backtracking via a continuation monad or explicit search stack, keeping the language surface clean. No language change needed.

comparisons.note: Full LP with backtracking and unification. Powerful for combinatorial search but the non-deterministic execution model is notoriously hard to reason about for programmers from imperative backgrounds.
comparisons.code:
path(X, Z) :- edge(X, Y), path(Y, Z).
?- path(1, Z).
Z = 2 ;
Z = 3.

comparisons.note: A minimal logic DSL embedded in a host language. It works but requires the programmer to think in a completely different evaluation model — the very friction Jet wants to avoid.
comparisons.code:
(run* (q)
  (fresh (x y)
    (== q (list x y))
    (membero x '(1 2))
    (membero y '(a b))))

decisions.title: Commit to a structural (AST/semantic) merge tool for Jet version control?
decisions.gist: Structural merge resolves version-control conflicts using the program's AST or semantic identity rather than line-based text diff. This is new and not yet carded for implementation. It depends on content-addressed definitions and a semantic index, neither of which is built.
decisions.explainer: Line-based merge fails when two branches rename a function, reorder arguments, or extract a helper — producing conflicts that are trivially safe or spurious conflicts that obscure real ones. A structural merge tool would compare AST nodes by identity (name + signature or content address), resolve renames and moves automatically, and surface only semantic conflicts. Prerequisites: stable AST serialization, content-addressed definitions (its own unbuilt card), and a semantic index API. This is a tooling feature, not a language feature — it does not touch syntax or sema, so I1/I8 are not at risk. But it is a large, standalone project that competes for capacity with in-flight compiler work.
decisions.story: I refactored a module across two branches — one renamed a function, the other added parameters. Git thinks it's a conflict. A structural merge tool would see they touched different things and merge cleanly.

options.name: Far-horizon: capture, don't build now
options.detail: Record the idea and its prerequisites (content-addressed defs, semantic index). Build neither until those foundations exist. The semantic index and content-addressed-definitions cards must land first; revisit structural merge after they do. No current action.

options.name: Build a structural merge tool now
options.detail: Start the tool alongside the compiler. Requires inventing an AST serialization format and a merge algorithm before the AST is stable. High risk of rework as the language evolves. Not recommended.

options.name: Reject — out of scope
options.detail: Structural merge is a tooling feature orthogonal to the language. Jet can ship v1 without it; existing Git workflows are sufficient. The effort is better spent on the compiler. Reject and don't revisit.
options.code:
// No action. Developers use standard git merge.
// Conflict resolution is a developer workflow problem, not a language problem.

comparisons.note: A structural diff tool using tree-sitter grammars. Shows diffs in terms of AST nodes rather than lines. Does not do merging — only diffing — but demonstrates the value of structural comparison.
comparisons.code:

decisions.title: Should Jet's runtime adapt behavior to environmental signals (battery, network, load, carbon)?
decisions.gist: The idea is a runtime that reads environmental conditions and adjusts behavior — throttles work on low battery, degrades quality under load, shifts tasks to low-carbon windows. This is a New idea with no existing card. The question is whether this belongs in the language/runtime or in a library that apps call.
decisions.explainer: Environmental adaptation is inherently app-specific policy — what 'degrade under load' means for a video encoder is different from a web server. Baking adaptation into the runtime (option B) risks making the default behavior magical and hard to audit (I1: safe/predictable defaults). A library that exposes signals (battery level, network quality, carbon intensity) and lets app code choose the policy is more composable and auditable. Carbon intensity data requires an external API (electricityMap, WattTime) — the runtime cannot self-contain it. This overlaps with D-ADAPTFID1 (fidelity knob) and D-CARBON1; all three should fold into one decision.
decisions.story: I'm shipping a background sync task. I want it to pause when the battery is below 20%, slow down on metered connections, and prefer running when the grid is clean — without writing platform-specific code for each.

options.name: Library exposing env signals + policy hooks
options.detail: Stdlib exposes a thin `Env` API: battery level, network quality, estimated carbon intensity (via OS/external). App code reads these and sets its own policy. Predictable, auditable, no hidden runtime behavior. Correct match for I1.

options.name: Runtime-managed adaptation
options.detail: The runtime automatically throttles tasks, degrades quality, or defers work based on environmental conditions. Magic and convenient but opaque — hard to debug when behavior differs across devices. Violates predictability (I1 concern).

options.name: Defer / don't add
options.detail: Niche use case. Most apps handle this ad-hoc or via platform APIs. Add only if there is clear demand. Fold the three adaptive cards (runtime, fidelity, carbon) into one decision when the time comes.
options.code: // No stdlib env-adaptation; apps use platform APIs directly

comparisons.note: Constraint-based scheduling (battery, network, idle) as library/framework, not language primitives. Policy is explicit in code.
OS signals exposed as library APIs; apps poll or observe and apply their own policy. No automatic adaptation.

decisions.title: Project formatter invocation, scope, ignore, and check semantics
decisions.gist: Choose how the existing zero-config Jet formatter expands from one file to projects, CI, stdin, VCS changes, and editors.
decisions.explainer:
Every option uses the same parser/formatter engine as LSP, Canvas, and single-file `jet fmt`. The choice is scope and command behavior. No multi-file filesystem transaction is falsely claimed: Jet preflights all files, stages sibling temporary files, replaces per file, and keeps a crash-recovery journal.

Fable hybrid review: All three options leave the CI contract vague: none separates 'needs formatting' from 'could not parse' in exit codes, none names stdin for editor diagnostics, and none states idempotence — the exact ambiguities behind years of prettier/rustfmt CI flakes. B makes the common project action a usage error and C rejects explicit paths, each hostile to one audience; the hybrid keeps A's discovery-plus-exact-scopes law and adds the exit-code triple, --stdin-path, one-pass preflight reporting, edition refusal, and the fixpoint guarantee, all consistent with ratified D-FMTPARENS1 engine behavior.
decisions.story: Inez formats one pasted file, checks a monorepo in CI, formats only her staged changes before commit, and expects her editor to produce byte-identical output without touching generated or vendored code.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet fmt
formatted 18 files
$ jet fmt --check --diff
clean
$ git add src/parser.jet
$ jet fmt --changed
decisions.detail: Recommended semantics: explicit files/directories format exactly that scope; no arguments finds the nearest enclosing workspace, else package, else the cwd tree. Workspace graph and VCS ignores exclude build/generated/vendor content and symlinks are not followed; an explicit ignored file is an expert override. Parse/preflight failure causes zero writes. Each replacement is atomic for that file; the journal detects and repairs a crash during a multi-file commit. `--check` never writes, exits 1 when changes are needed, and lists paths; `--diff` is valid only with `--check` and adds unified diffs. `--changed` means worktree, index, and untracked Jet files; `--changed=BASE` adds files changed from BASE plus local changes. It conflicts with explicit paths and stdin. `-` is the sole input and writes formatted source to stdout.

options.name: Hybrid project default with exact expert scopes
options.detail: No-arg formatting discovers workspace/package/cwd automatically. Explicit paths, stdin, CI check/diff, and VCS-changed modes provide exact control. The project graph, ignore law, staging, journal, output order, and exit codes are identical across CLI/editor/CI.
options.code:
jet fmt                         # nearest workspace/package, else cwd
jet fmt src tests               # exact explicit paths
jet fmt --check --diff          # no writes, exit 1 + unified diff
jet fmt --changed=origin/main   # base diff + index/worktree/untracked
jet fmt - < input.jet > output.jet

options.name: Explicit files and directories only
options.detail: `jet fmt` without paths prints usage; users or build tools choose every scope. Check, diff, changed, and stdin remain available. This avoids discovery surprises but makes the common project action ceremonial.
options.code:
jet fmt src tests
jet fmt --check src tests
jet fmt --changed
# bare jet fmt -> usage: supply PATH or --changed

options.name: Workspace/package only
options.detail: `jet fmt` always formats the nearest workspace or package according to its graph. Single explicit files use `jet fmt -` or editor formatting; arbitrary directory/path scopes are rejected. This is simple but weak for partial migrations and scripts.
options.code:
jet fmt                  # whole nearest workspace/package
jet fmt --check          # whole scope, CI
jet fmt src/one.jet      # error: project formatter does not accept partial paths

options.name: Project default with hardened exit, stdin-path, and idempotence law (hybrid)
options.detail: Adopts A's scope law verbatim (workspace/package/cwd discovery, explicit paths, `--check --diff`, `--changed`, stdin) and hardens the machine contract: exit 0 clean or formatted, 1 only when `--check` finds differences, 2 for usage, parse, or I/O errors, so CI distinguishes 'needs formatting' from 'broken'. `--check` lists paths sorted and root-relative; the existing global `--json` flag emits the stable machine report. Preflight reports every failing file in one pass before the zero-write abort; `--changed` outside version control is a diagnostic naming the fix, and a file declaring a newer edition than the engine knows is refused, never reformatted lossily. `jet fmt - --stdin-path=src/a.jet` names piped input for diagnostics and editor parity; stdin always formats, so the ignore law never applies to it. Output is a byte-identical fixpoint across CLI, LSP, Canvas, and CI — formatting twice equals formatting once.
options.code:
$ jet fmt --check --diff            # exit 1: differences; exit 2: parse/IO error
src/parser.jet
tests/lexer.jet
$ jet fmt - --stdin-path=src/a.jet < a.jet > out.jet
$ jet fmt --changed                  # outside a repo -> diagnostic with fix
$ jet fmt --check --json             # stable machine report for CI

comparisons.note: A canonical formatter plus project-aware tooling produces ecosystem consistency. Jet additionally preserves its ratified author choices and supplies one discoverable command.
File/stdin and Cargo project modes are useful but split across rustfmt and cargo fmt. Option A keeps one Jet command and one engine.

decisions.title: How much of the test suite CI runs, and when
decisions.gist: Pick what a green CI checkmark actually proves.
decisions.explainer: Work here lands directly on master, so push and merge are the same event — B's fast lane would gate nothing by itself. A makes the checkmark mean exactly one thing, which is the whole point once no strong reviewer stands behind it.
decisions.story: Priya lands a small formatter tweak late in the evening. CI goes green, she moves on. The formatter stability tests never ran — CI only executes 6 of the ~90 test targets — so the tweak silently drops a token when reprinting code, and the corruption ships. This exact failure lived in the repo for months once before. When the strongest reviewer is gone, the checkmark is the only reviewer left; this ballot decides what it means.
decisions.inWild:
$ git push
# GitHub Actions: ✓ CI passed (6 of ~90 test targets ran)

$ nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh
test fmt_stability_serde_markers ... FAILED
  expected: `name: text #[key]`
  emitted:  `name: text`        <- marker dropped, file corrupted on save

# Both of the above are true at the same time today.

options.name: Full suite on every push
options.detail: One lane, one meaning: CI runs verify-full.sh (all ~90 targets) on every push, with JET_REQUIRE_RUSTC=1 so environment self-skips fail loudly. A nightly lane adds rotating-seed fuzzing (N>=1000) and the perf ratchet. Green means the same thing as a local full-suite pass. Runs take tens of minutes; pushes are not blocked, only flagged.
options.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- name: Full suite
  run: nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh
  env: { JET_REQUIRE_RUSTC: 1 }

# nightly.yml (03:00)
- run: FUZZ_SEED=${{ github.run_id }} FUZZ_N=1000 nix develop -c cargo test --test fuzz_sema
- run: nix develop -c tools/perf/ci-perf-check.sh

$ git push   # ~25-40 min later:
✗ CI failed — fmt: fmt_stability_serde_markers

options.name: Fast push lane + full merge/nightly lane
options.detail: Every push runs a ~3-minute doc-sync tier (lib tests, truthfulness, decisions, diagnostics_coverage, snapshots). The full suite runs on master merges and nightly. Quick signal per push; the deep signal arrives within a day. Risk: with direct-to-master work, push and merge are the same event, so in practice the fast lane alone gates nothing.
options.code:
# push lane (~3 min)
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --lib --test truthfulness --test decisions \
        --test diagnostics_coverage --test diagnostic_snapshots
# master + nightly lane
- run: nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh

$ git push        # ✓ fast lane green in 3 min
# 03:00 nightly:  ✗ fmt stability failed — found the next morning

options.name: Keep the cherry-pick, fix the rot only
options.detail: Keep today's 6-target selection; repair the stale Tower step, add JET_REQUIRE_RUSTC, wire the perf check. The ~80 uncovered targets (fmt, ownership, repl, lsp, jetpack, ...) stay covered only by agents remembering to run verify-full.sh locally — the discipline dependency this epoch is trying to retire.
options.code:
# ci.yml unchanged in shape:
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test truthfulness
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test golden
# fmt/ownership/repl/lsp/... : still never run in CI

$ git push   # ✓ green — proves 6/90 targets

comparisons.note: PR CI runs a subset; nothing merges except through bors, which runs the full battery — merge green is total green.
comparisons.code: @bors r+   # queues full-suite gate before merge

comparisons.note: Fast premerge checks plus deep buildbots after landing; breakage found post-land is reverted by policy.
comparisons.code:
premerge: check-clang (fast)
buildbot: full stage2 + sanitizers (hours later)

decisions.title: Where maintainer helper commands live
decisions.gist: Pick the home for repo-maintainer tools: reduce, ice-report, snapshot bless, fixture scaffolds, fixture-path check.
decisions.explainer: Follows the ratified precedent (`jet devtools grammars`), keeps discovery in one --help screen, and adds no second binary. Beginner surface unaffected — devtools is already the maintainer shelf.
decisions.story: Sam is a maintainer (human or mid-tier agent) whose 400-line test program just crashed the compiler with the internal-error banner. Today the next step is hand-deleting statements one at a time to shrink the crash, then hand-copying expected output out of panic text to update fixtures — the two jobs where a weaker maintainer burns hours or gives up. These helpers make both mechanical; the ballot picks where they live. Whatever the spelling, none of it appears in beginner-facing help.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet run inventory.jet
internal compiler error: generated Rust rejected (I2)
this is a bug in jet — please report it

# Sam, today: open a 400-line file and start deleting lines by hand.
# Sam, after this card: one command produces a 10-line repro + report bundle.

options.name: jet devtools subcommands
options.detail: Extend the existing maintainer namespace that already holds `jet devtools grammars`: reduce, ice-report, bless, new-example, new-ui, check-fixture-paths. Discoverable in one place, ships with the compiler an agent already built, hidden from top-level `jet help` just like grammars is today.
options.code:
$ jet devtools reduce inventory.jet
reduced: 412 lines -> 11 lines (ICE preserved)  -> inventory.min.jet

$ jet devtools ice-report inventory.min.jet
wrote ice-report/: source, generated.rs, rustc.stderr, versions.txt

$ jet devtools new-ui move_out_of_view
created tests/ui/move_out_of_view.jet + .stderr (blessed)
reminder: add E-code row to docs/spec/diagnostics.md

options.name: Env vars + repo scripts only
options.detail: No new CLI surface: blessing via env vars on cargo test (UPDATE_EXPECT / JET_UPDATE_GOLDEN), reducer and scaffolds as scripts under scripts/dev/. Compiler binary untouched; tools only work from a repo checkout and are found by reading docs rather than --help.
options.code:
$ JET_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 nix develop -c cargo test --test golden
$ nix develop -c scripts/dev/reduce.sh inventory.jet
$ nix develop -c scripts/dev/new-ui.sh move_out_of_view

# discovery: ls scripts/dev/ + a docs table (no --help integration)

options.name: Separate jet-dev binary
options.detail: A second binary (cargo run -p jet-devtools or an installed jet-dev) holding all maintainer commands. Hard wall between user CLI and maintainer CLI — `jet help` can never leak a maintainer command — at the cost of a second entry point to version, build, and document.
options.code:
$ nix develop -c jet-dev reduce inventory.jet
$ nix develop -c jet-dev bless --ui move_out_of_view
$ nix develop -c jet-dev ice-report inventory.min.jet

# jet --help: unchanged, no devtools entry at all

comparisons.note: Maintainer tooling lives behind one entry point (x.py / bootstrap) plus cargo-bisect-rustc for reduction-style triage.
Maintainer commands ship inside the main tool under a namespace users never touch.
Standalone reducer proves the mechanical-reduction pattern this adopts.

decisions.title: Does the board refuse rule-breaking writes, or only report them?
decisions.gist: Pick how hard Tower enforces the working rules (done-gates, ballot completeness, owner-only actions).
decisions.explainer: The repeat offenders are agents, not you. C binds them at write time — prose rules become mechanical — while your phone workflow stays one tap. A ties your hands; B is today with extra steps.
decisions.story: An agent finishes step 2 of 5 on a card, marks it done, and moves on — the remaining steps evaporate until someone notices weeks later. Another agent files your acceptance verdict as a log note where you never see it again. Today every one of these writes succeeds, because the rules live in prose the agent may never have loaded. You have had to repeat these rules angrily more than once; this ballot decides whether the board itself starts saying no.
decisions.inWild:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
updated card #412 -> done        # 3 of 5 checklist items still open

$ tower decision add --title 'Cache strategy' --by helper-agent
added decision D-CACHE1          # no gist, no story, no options — reaches your queue empty

$ tower card activate '#413' --by helper-agent
activated #413                   # an owner-only action, performed by an agent

options.name: Hard gates for everyone
options.detail: The store refuses rule-breaking writes no matter who writes: done requires a complete checklist, ballots must be ballot-ready to enter the queue, ratify/activate demand owner attribution, frozen cards are read-only. Maximum consistency — but it also stops you: closing a card from your phone means ticking every box first, and there is no override when you just want something gone.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by owner
E_GATE: 3 checklist items unchecked — no done until complete (no override)

options.name: Lint-only, never refuse
options.detail: All writes keep succeeding; a `tower lint` sweep (run by agents, shown on the board) reports violations: done-with-open-checklist, empty ballots, mis-attributed ratifies. Zero friction — and zero protection at the moment of the write. A weak model that never runs lint recreates today exactly.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
updated card #412 -> done
$ tower lint
WARN #412 done with 3 unchecked items (by helper-agent)
WARN D-CACHE1 not ballot-ready: gist/story/options empty

options.name: Agent-hard, owner-soft
options.detail: Writes with --by other than owner hit hard gates: done-gate on checklists, ballot-ready validation (a --draft flag keeps drafts out of your queue), owner-only ratify/activate unless the agent quotes you explicitly (recorded in the event log), no writes to frozen/owner-lane cards, release of a building card requires a handoff note. Your own writes bypass everything. The rules bind exactly the population that keeps breaking them.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
E_GATE: 3 checklist items unchecked — complete them or --release --handoff "..."

$ tower decision ratify D-CACHE1 --outcome B --by helper-agent
E_OWNER: ratify is owner-only — use --on-behalf-of-owner "<owner's words>"

$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by owner
updated card #412 -> done        # owner bypass, no ceremony

comparisons.note: Branch protection blocks contributors while admins may bypass — the standard shape for solo-owner + helpers.
comparisons.code:
Require status checks: on
Include administrators: off

comparisons.note: Hooks enforce by default with an explicit, visible escape.
The compiler refuses at the moment of the mistake instead of reporting it later — the reason the invariant holds in practice.

decisions.title: Where ratified decisions and done cards go to rest
decisions.gist: Whether finished board history stays inside tower.json or moves to a separate archive file, and what triggers the move.
decisions.explainer: A keeps you in control of when history moves (matching how you already close out epochs), keeps one mental model (tower.json = the board), and shrinks writes, backups, git churn, and phone payload all at once. B is the same end-state but moves things the instant they close — done cards vanish from the Board's Done lists into a second file mid-session. C treats the symptom (transport) and leaves the file growing forever.
decisions.story: Nate opens Tower on his phone after a ballot session. The board file is 4.2 MB, and 68% of it is history: 496 already-ratified decisions (1.7 MB) and 305 done cards (1.1 MB). Every single write — even a one-line log entry — rewrites all 4.2 MB, snapshots another 4.2 MB backup (backups/ is at 82 MB), pushes the full state over the live stream to his phone, and lands another multi-megabyte version of tower.json in git (356 versions and counting). The live working set he actually looks at is about 0.4 MB.
decisions.inWild:
$ du -h .tower/tower.json
4.2M    .tower/tower.json

$ tower state | jq '.decisions | length'
496        # every one already ratified — zero open

$ tower state | jq '[.cards[] | select(.phase=="done")] | length'
305        # of 434 cards total

$ du -h .tower/backups
82M     .tower/backups    # 20 rolling copies of the full file

$ git log --oneline -- .tower/tower.json | wc -l
356        # full-file versions in repo history
decisions.detail: Q: Does archiving lose anything?  A: No — archived items stay on disk in .tower/, stay in git, and stay greppable; they just leave the hot file. Q: Can an archived decision be reopened?  A: Yes, via an explicit restore that moves it back into tower.json first. Q: What about the docs? Ballot text for ratified syntax already lives durably in docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md; the archive is the raw record.

options.name: Explicit archive command, epoch-aligned
options.detail: New `tower archive` verb moves ratified decisions, done cards (with their questions), and events older than 30 days into .tower/archive/<epoch>.json — one file per epoch, append-only, committed to git. Run it by hand or let closing an epoch run it automatically. `tower archive list/show/restore <id>` reads it back; `tower card show` on an archived card still works (reads the archive transparently). The owner decides when history moves; nothing disappears on its own.
options.code:
$ tower archive run --by owner
archived: 496 decisions, 291 done cards, 1712 events → .tower/archive/e1.json … e6.json
tower.json: 4.2M → 0.5M

$ tower archive show D-MEM1
D-MEM1  ratified 2026-07-03 → A  (archive/e5.json)

$ tower archive restore '#188' --by owner
restored card #188 (+2 decisions) into the live board

options.name: Auto-retire on close (split live/history files)
options.detail: No command to remember: the moment a decision is ratified or a card verified done, the store writes it to .tower/history.json (append-only ledger) and drops it from tower.json on the next write. tower.json permanently contains only live work. The Board's 'Done' subgroups render from the ledger lazily. Reopen = automatic restore. History is never more than one write behind; the hot file never grows again.
options.code:
$ tower decision ratify D-X1 --outcome A --by owner
ratified D-X1 → A   (retired to history.json)

$ du -h .tower/tower.json .tower/history.json
0.4M    .tower/tower.json     # only live work, forever
5.8M    .tower/history.json   # append-only, grows cold

$ tower card show '#42'        # a done card
#42  done  (from history)  …full card, log intact…

options.name: Keep one file; slim what moves
options.detail: tower.json stays the single complete record. Instead, stop moving the whole file around: SSE frames send only diffs, backups are gzipped (4.2 MB → ~0.4 MB each), and the UI loads done cards/ratified decisions on demand. Git history still carries the full file, and every write still rewrites 4.2 MB locally, but network, phone, and backup weight drop to near-live-set size.
options.code:
$ du -h .tower/backups
8.1M    .tower/backups        # 20 gzipped snapshots

# SSE frame after a log entry (diff, not full state):
data: {"rev":2482,"patch":[{"op":"add","path":"/cards/12/log/0",
       "value":{"at":"2026-07-10","by":"claude-main","text":"started"}}]}

$ du -h .tower/tower.json
4.2M    .tower/tower.json     # unchanged, keeps growing

comparisons.note: Completed issues auto-archive after a configurable window; they leave every view but stay searchable and restorable. Nobody scrolls past them again.
comparisons.code: Settings → Projects → Auto-archive completed issues: after 1 month

comparisons.note: Same shape as loose objects vs packfiles: the hot working set stays small, history compacts into cold files that are still fully readable.

decisions.comment: But enforce stricter "done" testing & keep a buffer of decisions made pre ratification so I can walk them back before ratification if needed

decisions.title: How an agent gets its marching orders from Tower
decisions.gist: Whether starting work on a card takes one command that returns everything, a generated brief file, or native harness tools.
decisions.explainer: A collapses the error-prone five-step ritual into one call that cannot omit the ratification comment or an open question, and it works identically for Claude, codex, and bare scripts. B helps only harnesses with auto-load; C is a strong later layer on top of A (same packet, typed transport).
decisions.story: A fresh Claude session is told 'work the board'. Today it runs five commands (status, next, card show, decision list, question list), re-reads the skill doc to remember the phase rules, and only then starts. Every extra step is a place a sub-agent skips something — the cards that bounced usually bounced because the agent never saw a ratification comment or an open question sitting right on the card.
decisions.inWild:
# today: five reads before any work happens
$ tower status
$ tower next --epoch e3
$ tower card show '#412'
$ tower decision list --card '#412' --json
$ tower question list --open
# …and the ratification comment on D-X1 is 40 lines deep in JSON
# the agent never printed
decisions.detail: Q: Does this change what the owner does? A: No — pure agent surface. Q: Does it replace the skill doc? A: The rules footer travels with the packet, so a sub-agent that only ever sees the packet still knows the phase-honesty rules.

options.name: One-shot work packet: `tower brief`
options.detail: One command claims the next card (or a named one) and prints the complete packet: card body + plan, every linked decision with outcome AND the owner's ratification comment, open questions, blockers, related doc paths found in the body, and a 5-line rules footer (phase honesty, --by, expect-rev). --json for machines. A sub-agent brief becomes literally `tower brief '#412' --agent jet-impl-1`.
options.code:
$ tower brief --agent claude-main
━ #412 P1 building — Computed module fields (e3, m-comptime)
  plan: 1. parser field-expr 2. sema eval gate 3. golden
  decisions:
    D-CTMARKER1 = C  «comptime { } block + $ splice»
    owner comment: "C, but the block must nest — see my note"
  open questions: q88 [owner] "does this break pack.jet imports?"
  blocked by: —
  docs: docs/plans/epoch-5/unified-ecosystem.md
  rules: log every advance --by claude-main · verify≠builder ·
         done only after full suite green

options.name: Rendered brief file the harness auto-loads
options.detail: `tower serve` (or a githook) keeps .tower/BRIEF.md rendered with the current agent-lane queue and per-card packets. Harnesses that auto-load context files (CLAUDE.md include, AGENTS.md pointer) pull it in for free — zero commands at session start. The file is a read-only view; writes still go through the CLI.
options.code:
$ head .tower/BRIEF.md
# Tower brief — rev 2481 (auto-generated, read-only)
## Next up
1. #412 building — Computed module fields
   decisions: D-CTMARKER1=C ("C, but the block must nest…")
   open: q88 "does this break pack.jet imports?"
2. #405 verify — REPL Ctrl-C exit

# CLAUDE.md gains one line:
@.tower/BRIEF.md

options.name: Native tools: Tower as an MCP server
options.detail: `tower serve --mcp` exposes tower_next / tower_brief / tower_update / tower_ballot as typed tools. Claude and other MCP harnesses call the board without shelling out (no nix wrapper, no JSON quoting), and every write is schema-validated at the tool boundary. Shell CLI remains for humans and scripts.
options.code:
// agent-side tool call, no shell involved
tower_brief({ agent: "claude-main" })
→ { card: "#412", phase: "building",
    decisions: [{ id: "D-CTMARKER1", outcome: "C",
                  comment: "C, but the block must nest — see my note" }],
    questions: [{ id: "q88", text: "does this break pack.jet imports?" }],
    rules: ["log advances --by", "verify≠builder", "suite green before done"] }

comparisons.note: `gh issue view` prints the issue, labels, comments, and linked PRs in one call — the packet pattern, and the reason agents drive GitHub well.

decisions.title: Exit criteria live on the card and gate 'done'
decisions.gist: How a card proves it is finished: a checklist the CLI enforces, an acceptance ballot for you, or both for flagged cards.
decisions.explainer: C gives every card a mechanical floor (no more done-by-assertion) and reserves your time for the cards where your eye is the acceptance test — which is exactly where the bounces have happened. A alone leaves your verdicts informal; B alone makes you the bottleneck on all 400+ cards.
decisions.story: The frontend cards bounced twice because 'done' was claimed from the builder's own summary — no feature-by-feature evidence against the full mock, no independent check, and your acceptance verdict ended up in a card log where no process saw it. Today a card's exit criteria live in prose (body, plan, or nowhere), so nothing mechanical stops verify→done while half the list is unmet.
decisions.inWild:
# card #360, bounce round 2 — the criteria existed only as prose:
$ tower card show '#360' | jq -r .body | tail -3
Done requires feature-by-feature matrix vs FULL hybrid.html
with owner comments, verified in the owner's real terminal.

$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by builder-agent
updated card #360 → done      # nothing checked any of that
decisions.detail: Q: Who writes the criteria? A: The planning agent, when the plan is written; you can add/edit items from the card modal. Q: Does this add owner work? A: Only where you opt a card in — everything else is agent-side enforcement.

options.name: Machine-checked criteria list
options.detail: Cards get a criteria[] field: numbered items, each open → met (builder) → verified (a different agent, recorded). `--phase done` is rejected while any item is unverified, and the verifier must differ from the assignee. The card modal shows the checklist with per-item state.
options.code:
$ tower card criteria '#360' --add "matrix vs full hybrid.html, per feature" --by planner
$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by builder-agent
tower: E_CRITERIA — 2 of 5 criteria unverified (3,5); verifier must not be the builder

$ tower card verify '#360' --meet 3 --evidence "pty run + screenshot, all 14 features" --by jet-verify
$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by jet-verify
updated card #360 → done

options.name: Acceptance ballot on every close
options.detail: Closing any card auto-mints a one-option-per-verdict acceptance ballot for you (accept / bounce with comment), with the evidence summary as the ballot body. Done = you ratify. Your verdicts become durable decisions instead of log lines — but every card now waits on you.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#360' --phase verify --by jet-verify
minted D-ACCEPT-360: "Accept #360?"  → your Now queue

# your phone, focus mode:
D-ACCEPT-360  Accept #360 — frontend matrix
  evidence: 14/14 features vs hybrid.html, terminal transcript attached
  [A] Accept   [B] Bounce (comment required)

options.name: A + acceptance ballot only where flagged
options.detail: Criteria list enforced everywhere (option A), and cards you flag with needs-acceptance additionally mint the acceptance ballot on close — owner-facing surfaces get your verdict as a ballot, plumbing cards close on verified criteria alone. Matches how you already ruled that sign-off verdicts must be ballots, without putting all 400 cards through your queue.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#360' --needs-acceptance --by owner   # once, at greenlight
…builder meets criteria, verifier verifies…
$ tower card update '#360' --phase done --by jet-verify
minted D-ACCEPT-360 → your Now queue    # flagged card

$ tower card update '#405' --phase done --by jet-verify
updated card #405 → done                # unflagged: criteria were enough

comparisons.note: Required reviews + status checks: merges are blocked mechanically, and review-by-author is impossible. The branch protection model, applied to cards.
comparisons.code: Settings → Branches → Require review from someone other than the author

decisions.title: Board view rebuilt for a 434-card project
decisions.gist: What the Board tab becomes now that Agents is gone: a progress roadmap, a dense worklist table, or a search-first spotlight.
decisions.explainer: Your two Board jobs are progress-scan and planning passes; A makes the first instant (burndown per epoch/milestone, computed from the event log Tower already keeps) and keeps active cards one glance deep. B optimizes bulk re-ordering you do rarely; C optimizes find, which ⌘K already covers.
decisions.story: Nate opens Board to answer one question — 'where is epoch 3 actually at, and what is moving?' — and gets a wall of collapsible accordions: 8 epochs, hundreds of tiles, Done subgroups he has to expand one by one. On the phone it is minutes of scrolling. The two things he does here (scan progress, find one card) are both slow, and neither shows burndown over time.
decisions.inWild:
# what the board holds today
$ tower status
  TOWER · Jet · epoch e3 · rev 2481
  cards: 434 total — 129 active, 305 done
  epochs: 8, milestones: 2

# owner's actual questions, unanswered by the current view:
#  - is e3 burning down or stalled this week?
#  - which milestone is at risk?
#  - what did agents move today?
decisions.detail: Q: Does Now change? A: No — Now stays the decide/greenlight queue; this ballot is only the Board tab. Q: Do card modals change? A: No. All three options keep ⌘K and the card modal exactly as they are.

options.name: Roadmap ledger — progress is the page
options.detail: Board becomes a vertical roadmap: one row per epoch with a burndown sparkline (done/total over the last 30 days, computed from events), milestone bars underneath, and only ACTIVE cards shown inline, grouped by lane. Done and frozen live on a per-epoch 'ledger' page one tap away. The page answers 'how is it going' before you scroll.
options.code:
BOARD
  E3 syntax core          ████████████░░░  118/141 · ▂▃▅▆▇ this week +9
    m: memory-v5 ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓░ 7/9      m: comptime ▓▓░░ 2/6 ⚠ stalled 6d
    building(3)  #412 computed modules [claude-main]  …
    verify(2)    #405 repl ctrl-c  …
    → ledger: 118 done, 4 frozen
  E7 native-jetos         ██░░░░░░░░░░░░░  12/63 · ▁▁▂▃▃ +3

options.name: Ops table — the board as a worklist
options.detail: Board becomes one dense sortable table: every active card is a row (num, title, lane, priority, order, assignee, epoch, updated), click a header to sort, type to filter, inline-edit lane/priority/order without opening the modal. The fastest way to re-order work and spot stale rows; progress lives in a slim header strip.
options.code:
#    title                     lane      pri  ord  who          upd
  412  computed module fields    building  P1   1    claude-main  today
  405  repl ctrl-c exits         verify    P1   2    jet-verify   today
  399  fan-out namespace axis    plan      P2   —    —            6d ⚠
  [filter: e3 · sort: order ↑ · 129 rows]

options.name: Spotlight board — search-first, no scroll
options.detail: Board opens as a full-page search/filter box with saved views as chips (My queue · E3 active · Stalled >5d · Recently done). No accordion tree at all: you type or tap a chip and get exactly that slice as cards. The board is a query surface; nothing renders until asked, which also makes it the fastest view on a phone.
options.code:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ▸ find: "comptime"                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
 [My queue] [E3 active] [Stalled >5d] [Done this week]

  #412 computed module fields   building  P1  claude-main
  #155 comptime block           done      P1
  2 matches · 12ms

comparisons.note: Cycle view leads with a burndown graph and only in-cycle issues; archive is elsewhere. Closest to option A.
Terminal ops-table archetype of option B: one sortable table, inline edits, no navigation.
