decisions.title: Add generic modules (ML-functor-style module parameterized by a type or value)?
decisions.gist: Jet has generic types and functions. Generic modules — a module parameterized by a type or value at the module level, instantiated to produce a new module — do not exist. This decides whether to add them or keep the surface at generic types and functions only.
decisions.explainer: ML-style functors let you write `module Map(K: Ord)` and instantiate it as `module IntMap = Map(Int)`. The result is a new module with all members specialized to `K = Int`. In Jet, generic types already handle the common case (`Map[K: Ord, V]`); generic modules go further by allowing module-level abstraction (sharing multiple related types, hiding implementation modules, enforcing interface contracts at the module boundary). Under I8, if generic types already cover the use case, a second mechanism is a strike. The complexity is high: module instantiation affects name resolution, the module graph, and comptime. There is no ratified syntax precedent in Jet for module-level generics.
decisions.story: I'm building a pluggable hash-map where the key comparison strategy is a module (not just a function). I want `module HashMap(K: KeyModule)` where `KeyModule` supplies `hash`, `eq`, and an associated `Error` type — none of which are cleanly expressible as a single generic type parameter.

options.name: Add generic modules (ML-functor style)
options.detail: Ratify module-level parameterization. A module can declare type/value parameters; instantiation produces a new named module. Requires new syntax, new name-resolution rules, and comptime integration. Only justified if a concrete use case cannot be served by generic types alone.

options.name: Keep generic types and functions only (status quo)
options.detail: The existing `Type[T: Trait]` and `fn foo[T: Trait]()` cover the overwhelming majority of parameterization needs. Module-level generics add complexity for a narrow use case. Reject until a concrete case proves generic types are insufficient. I8-clean.

options.name: Defer pending concrete use case
options.detail: Don't reject outright — park the card until a real Jet codebase hits the wall with generic types and functions and needs functor-level abstraction. Then revisit with a concrete motivating example.
options.code:
// deferred: no syntax or implementation
// reopen when a concrete stdlib or user case requires it

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are the canonical ML-functor. `module Map.Make(Ord)` produces a map module specialized to `Ord.t`. Widely used but notoriously hard to read for newcomers.
comparisons.code:
module IntMap = Map.Make(Int)
let m = IntMap.add 1 "one" IntMap.empty

comparisons.note: Rust has no module generics — generic types and traits cover the use case. This is the status-quo model Jet already follows; it has proven sufficient for a production systems language.
comparisons.code:
// No generic modules; use generic structs + traits:
struct HashMap<K: [Hash, Eq], V> { ... }

decisions.title: What exact syntax distinguishes generic-module type parameters, value parameters, and instantiation?
decisions.gist: Before choosing a spelling: resolve the conflict with D-GENMOD1's floor example (paren type params) and D-LINALG1's blessed `<N>` value-in-angles. The current option set contains no choice that is consistent with both prior decisions simultaneously. A new option (annotation-kind in `<...>`, no extra keyword) resolves both. The "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling may also close Options A–C entirely; confirm its scope before proceeding.
decisions.explainer: Owner instruction integrated: Jet generics use `<T>`, so generic modules must not invent `[]` for type parameters. Adversarial pass: mixing type and value parameters can become C++-template soup or force users to guess whether an argument is a type or value. Patch: keep type parameters in `<...>`, keep compile-time value parameters in `(...)`, and require instantiation to mirror declaration. If that still feels too large for E3, choose the Epoch 6 defer option and keep ordinary generic structs/functions as the only generic surface for now.
decisions.story: Priya is writing a fixed-size LRU cache package. The key type controls hashing/equality, while the capacity is a compile-time value. She wants one generic module that exports `Cache`, `put`, and `get`, then instantiates `StringCache32` once for the rest of the package.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Address GENMOD2; integrate the instruction that Jet generics use `<T>`, provide better options, and include an option to defer to Epoch 6.
Agent answer: Corrected. The previous `[]` type-parameter option was wrong for Jet because `[]` already reads as list/indexing while `<T>` is the ratified generic form. Updated options now center `<T>` for type parameters, separate compile-time value parameters with `(...)`, and add an Epoch 6 defer option.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): PRIOR DECISION CONFLICTS (must resolve before any option is adopted): D-GENMOD1's ratified code example uses `module Sorted(T: Ord)` — type param in parens; Option A contradicts this. D-LINALG1 blessed Vec<N> (value-in-<...>) as the substrate spelling; Option A puts values in (...), directly contradicting. The comptime section of syntax-decisions.md says "Rejected: const generics in v1" — module value parameters are const generics and this rejection may apply. PARSER HAZARD (Option A): `Lru<String>(32)` is syntactically identical to D-SERDE6 turbofish `fn<T>(arg)`; parser cannot resolve without name-resolution, violating parse-before-sema. VOCABULARY HAZARD (Option B): `const` is a teaching-error-only keyword (S14); using it inside `<...>` is the first real use. MISSING OPTION E: unified `<K: Hash, capacity: Int>` with annotation-kind as distinguisher — consistent with D-LINALG1, avoids all vocabulary collisions.

options.name: Unified `<...>`: annotation kind distinguishes type vs value params (recommended)
options.detail: Both type and value parameters live in `<...>`. A parameter whose annotation is a bound/trait (`K: Hash`) is a type parameter; one whose annotation is a value type (`capacity: Int`) is a value parameter — no extra keyword, no dual-bracket syntax. Instantiation mirrors declaration: `Lru<String, 32>`. Consistent with D-LINALG1's `Vec<N>` substrate (value-in-angles already blessed). Supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example which used parens — that was explicitly a placeholder "until GENMOD2 decides." Parser: distinguishes a type expression (capital-cased, D-CASING1) from a value expression at instantiation sites in `<...>` — mostly mechanical at the lexer level.

options.name: Defer generic modules to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not add module-level type/value parameters now. Ordinary generic structs and functions (`fn sort<T: Ord>`, `struct Vec<T>`) already cover most use cases. Defer if the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling in the comptime section applies to module value parameters, or if the D-LINALG1 `Vec<N>` value-parameter surface needs a unified ruling before any single site commits.

options.name: Ordinary generic types/fns only — no module-level parameters
options.detail: Decline generic modules entirely. Priya's LRU cache is a generic struct with a capacity field; the type-level instantiation story is solved by generic types already. Module-level parameters are a second mechanism for the same parametrization job (I8 risk). Only reconsider if a concrete use case cannot be expressed with generic types.

comparisons.note: Rust uses `<T>` for type parameters and also has const generics in `<...>`. Good precedent for Option B, but Jet should avoid forcing values into type syntax unless needed.
C++ templates mix type and value parameters in angle brackets. Powerful, but visually dense and a known complexity sink.
comparisons.code: template<typename K, int N> struct Lru { ... };

comparisons.note: OCaml functors are module-level generics, but parameters are module-shaped. Powerful, less beginner-direct than Jet’s desired package surface.
Zig uses comptime parameters in function-like declarations; clear for values, but Jet already has `<T>` for type generics.
comparisons.code: fn Lru(comptime K: type, comptime capacity: usize) type { ... }

Consistent with D-LINALG1's Vec<N>; supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype floor example. If the "const generics in v1 rejected" ruling applies, choose Option B (defer).

decisions.title: REPL Core effect authorization
decisions.gist: Choose how existing Jet effects are authorized inside the REPL.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has one effect language: D-EFF4's roots, D-EFFTREE1 paths, lexical #Grant regions, and invocation policy through the existing --allow-fs/--allow-env/--allow-exec/--allow-net/--allow-io/--allow-time/--allow-rand flags. This ballot adds no REPL-specific grant names, grant commands, or persistent permission store. All options keep Core's current static bare-root tags; they do not globally retag Core with compiler-minted leaves. Dynamic capability data distinguishes resources and operations beneath a statically proven root. Thus an Env capability may permit reading HOME but not writing HOME; an Exec capability for one pinned Exec.Run target never permits Exec.Exit; an Io capture channel never permits terminal input. The canonical REPL filesystem root is fixed once: `jet repl --project DIR` uses the canonical project root, otherwise the process's starting cwd. The evaluator opens that root as a directory handle before accepting input. A symlink used to reach the starting location is resolved once when opening the root; later path components are descriptor-relative and no-follow. Because `core.os` has no current static effect root and this ballot does not retag Core, every `core.os` operation remains native-only E1802 in the REPL, including host facts and `set_current_dir`; therefore evaluated code cannot mutate cwd, and the fixed root handle never changes. --allow-fs is only the existing Fs invocation ceiling and never broadens reach beyond that fixed root. Every file operation uses verified handles; if the platform cannot enforce race-safe confinement it fails closed. Process execution pins executable identity before authorization, never re-resolves PATH, uses a verified cwd and minimal declared environment, bounds time, forwards interrupt, kills/reaps children, and separately authorizes redirects. Network authority pins scheme, hostname, port, and resolved addresses; redirects or new DNS results require fresh authority. Env.Read and Env.Write are dynamically separate exact-key resources under bare Env; session authorization for one key/direction never covers another. Ambient Time operations (wall clock, local zone, sleep, stopwatch/instant) require Time; a Clock created from an explicit seed/value is injected data and needs no ambient authority. Ambient/OS and secure randomness require Rand; an explicitly seeded Rng is injected data and needs none. `core.crypto.random` remains E1802 while it is native-only; if the interpreter gains it, it follows secure Rand policy. REPL-owned stdout/stderr capture is inherent evaluator plumbing: print/eprint and subprocess Capture write only to the REPL's captured output and require no runtime Io authority. Reading stdin, raw terminal access, inheriting/streaming a subprocess terminal, or redirecting to an external stream requires #Grant(Io) plus Io policy. A subprocess file redirect requires Fs for the verified file handle; Capture alone grants neither Io nor Fs. FFI, tasks, raw memory, display/UI backends, servers, and other native-only facilities remain E1802. Missing lexical authority remains E0712. E1802 remains only for unavailable interpreter features. This decision allocates E1803 to REPL runtime-policy denial, missing invocation policy, or confinement failure after lexical proof. E1803 must be registered in diagnostics with what/why/fix and pinned by a UI snapshot before implementation uses it.
decisions.story: Maya is learning Jet in a cloned service. She wraps a config read in the same #Grant(Fs) construct used by checked programs, then pastes a formatter command. Static checking proves which effect roots the turn can reach, but the REPL must still decide which real project file or executable that erased capability may touch. Maya needs the safe choice explained at the moment it matters. Dev needs the same effect proof with explicit invocation flags in a scripted session, without learning a REPL-only authorization system.

options.name: Prompted invocation policy
options.detail: Require an enclosing #Grant(root) for every effectful turn. In an interactive TTY, when the corresponding existing --allow-root policy was not supplied, pause before each not-yet-authorized external operation and offer once, session, or deny. Once covers exactly the displayed operation/resource tuple and is discarded before execution, so success or failure cannot retain it. Session stores exactly `(root effect, operation kind, resource identity/scope)` in memory: Env.Read HOME does not cover Env.Write HOME, Exec.Run tool A does not cover tool B or Exec.Exit, and a multi-resource turn prompts separately in execution order before performing each newly reached operation. On reuse, the same authorization preflight names the matching session allowance and offers continue or revoke; revoke deletes that tuple before the operation and returns to once/session/deny. This prompt/preflight is the sole inspection and revocation surface, not a second permission mechanism. All session tuples disappear on REPL exit or restart. Existing --allow-root flags skip ordinary root prompts for that invocation but do not relax confinement or lexical #Grant; non-TTY never prompts and requires the corresponding flag. Exec.Exit is never subsumed by Exec.Run, a session tuple, or --allow-exec: every interactive exit gets a separate `[y/N]` consequence prompt, while non-TTY requires #Grant(Exec) plus --allow-exec and exits without prompting. Recommended: beginner authority stays contextual and safe, experts get auditable flags, and both use Jet's one effect model. All shared confinement, pinning, Env, Time, Rand, Io, diagnostic, and native-only invariants above apply. Process Capture is inherent REPL output; Inherit/Stream/file redirects require their separately proven Io/Fs roots and policies.
options.code:
$ jet repl --project /work/api
user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Core effect Fs requests runtime authority before this operation.
  operation: read
  target:    config.toml
  confined:  /work/api (descriptor-relative, no symlinks)
  [o] once  [s] exact tuple for this session  [d] deny
s
port = 8080 : Result

user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Using session Fs.Read authority for `config.toml`. [c] continue  [r] revoke
c
port = 8080 : Result

user> use core.env as env
ok
user> #Grant(Env) { caps -> env.get("HOME") }
Core effect Env requests runtime authority: Read key HOME. [o] once  [s] exact tuple for session  [d] deny
s
/work/api : Option
user> #Grant(Env) { caps -> env.set("HOME", "/tmp") }
Core effect Env requests runtime authority: Write key HOME. [o] once  [s] exact tuple for session  [d] deny
d
Error [E1803]: Env.Write for `HOME` was denied
 Why: session authority covers Env.Read for this key, not mutation
 Fix: choose once or session only if this write is intended

user> use core.process as process
ok
user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.run(["jet", "fmt", "build/preview.jet"]) }
Core effect Exec requests runtime authority before this operation.
  executable: /work/api/.jet/toolchain/bin/jet (identity pinned)
  argv:       jet fmt build/preview.jet
  cwd:        /work/api
  env:        minimal declared environment
  timeout:    30s
  redirects:  Capture (inherent REPL output; no Io grant)
  [o] once  [s] exact Exec.Run tuple for session  [d] deny
o
ProcessResult(code: 0, output: , errors: ) : Result

user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.exit(7) }
Core effect Exec requests orderly REPL exit with status 7. [y/N]
y
# terminal restored; children reaped; REPL exits 7

$ printf 'use core.files as files\n#Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }\n' | jet repl --allow-fs
port = 8080 : Result

options.name: Flags only
options.detail: Require #Grant(root) in the turn and the corresponding existing --allow-root flag at REPL startup. Never prompt and never persist policy. The flag opens only that bare-root invocation ceiling; each lexical capability remains dynamically narrowed to the concrete operation/resource. All shared confinement, root fixation, process/network pinning, Env key/direction, Time/Clock, Rand/Rng, Io/Capture, diagnostic, and native-only invariants above apply independently. Thus --allow-env plus #Grant(Env) may perform the exact Env.Read/Env.Write operation reached, seeded Clock/Rng need no flag, Capture needs no --allow-io, Inherit/Stream need #Grant(Io) plus --allow-io, and a file redirect also needs #Grant(Fs) plus --allow-fs. A missing flag reports E1803 after lexical proof. Exec.Exit is a distinct operation never obtained from an Exec.Run resource capability; under this flags-only option it requires #Grant(Exec) plus --allow-exec, performs orderly cleanup, and never prompts. Without both it cannot terminate anything. This is maximally predictable for automation and experts, but beginners must understand invocation policy before their first ambient operation.
options.code:
$ jet repl
user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Error [E1803]: this REPL invocation does not allow Fs
 Why: #Grant proves lexical authority, but host policy did not pass --allow-fs
 Fix: restart with `jet repl --allow-fs`; access remains confined to the REPL root

$ jet repl --allow-fs --allow-exec
user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
port = 8080 : Result
user> use core.process as process
ok
user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.exit(0) }
# orderly exit: terminal restored, children reaped, status 0

$ printf 'use core.files as files\n#Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }\n' | jet repl --allow-fs
port = 8080 : Result

options.name: Pure REPL only
options.detail: The REPL executes pure Core plus deterministic injected Clock/Rng values only. #Grant remains valid Jet syntax, but external Fs, Env, Exec, Net, Io input, ambient Time, and ambient Rand are intentionally unavailable in this interpreter and therefore report current E1802 with the jet run/build escape. Existing --allow-* flags do not widen the REPL. No dynamic resource capabilities or persistence exist. Exec.Exit is the sole control exception: process.exit(code) does not require host Exec authority and is interpreted as an orderly REPL quit after terminal restoration; process.run/cmd/pipeline remain E1802. This draws the strongest boundary but rejects the accepted goal of exploring side-effect-safe Core in place.
options.code:
$ jet repl
user> use core.encoding.json as json
ok
user> json.parse("{\"port\":8080}")
Data(fields: [port: 8080]) : Result

user> use core.files as files
ok
user> #Grant(Fs) { caps -> files.read("config.toml") }
Error [E1802]: the REPL interpreter cannot run `core.files.read()`
 Why: this option keeps external Fs unavailable even inside #Grant
 Fix: put the code in a file and use `jet run`; --allow-fs does not widen the REPL

user> use core.process as process
ok
user> #Grant(Exec) { caps -> process.exit(0) }
# orderly REPL quit; terminal restored

$ jet repl --allow-exec
error: --allow-exec does not widen a pure-only REPL

comparisons.note: Deno separates filesystem, environment, process, and network policy and supports prompts or flags. Jet differs by requiring its existing lexical #Grant proof as well as invocation policy, and by attaching resource limits to capability handles.
comparisons.code:
Deno: --allow-read=./config --allow-net=api.example.com
Jet: #Grant(Fs) { caps -> ... } plus --allow-fs or the option-A prompt

comparisons.note: Capability-oriented filesystems operate relative to an already-open directory handle. This avoids the check-then-open race and symlink swap that realpath-prefix sandboxes miss.
comparisons.code: root_fd -> open child component with no-follow -> operate on returned handle

comparisons.note: Common REPLs inherit ambient host authority. Pasted code can mutate files/environment, launch subprocesses, or connect to the network without a lexical capability proof.
Pure evaluation rejects ambient effects unless impurity is explicitly enabled. This informs option C and the deterministic non-TTY rule in A/B.

decisions.comment: I want to be able to use flags regardless, this way it will be better ux for people who want the language to get out of the way if they know what theyre doing

decisions.title: Place fuzz and LSP in the frequency-ringed CLI
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical homes for the two native commands omitted from D-CLI-SURFACE1's exhaustive rings.
decisions.explainer: Recommend A: fuzzing is part of the test/dev loop and stays flat; LSP is self/tooling infrastructure and moves under `jet self`. The editor integrations change atomically, and bare `jet lsp` becomes the same immediate teaching error required for every moved verb.
decisions.story: Maya fuzzes a parser before release and her editor launches Jet's language server automatically. D-CLI-SURFACE1 precisely names every flat daily verb and every grouped long-tail verb, but today's registry also contains `fuzz` and `lsp`. An implementer cannot remove, group, or retain either spelling without inventing user-facing command law.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet lsp                 # launched by VS Code/Zed, normally not typed

# D-CLI-SURFACE1 currently assigns neither command a destination.
decisions.detail: This ballot only closes D-CLI-SURFACE1=B's two-command omission. It does not reopen its four groups, daily list, or no-alias rule. EngineDispatch front doors (`env`, `push`, `trust`, `bridge`, `services`, `image`, `os`, `config`, `outdated`, `search`, `info`, `logs`, `clean`) remain outside #468's native-verb shrink exactly as the card scoped them; existing product decisions own them. `jet ?`, help, man, completions, shell completion, editor installers, docs, tests and external-command collision checks must all read the same nested registry. A moved spelling is intercepted before external `jet-<name>` discovery, emits E2101 with What/Why/Fix, preserves all following argv verbatim in the printed replacement, exits 2, performs no action, and is never an alias. `--json` emits the existing diagnostic schema with replacement argv. No L2001 deprecation window applies: D-CLI-SURFACE1 explicitly chose teaching errors rather than compatibility aliases. Beginner pass: fuzz remains discoverable beside test; editor setup hides LSP plumbing. Expert pass: `jet self lsp --bench/doctor` retains exact flags and stdio behavior. Hybrid pass: one registry entry owns canonical argv plus migration metadata; generators cannot drift.

options.name: Flat fuzz; self lsp
options.detail: Keep `jet fuzz` in the daily developer ring. Move the machine-facing server to `jet self lsp`; update every first-party editor/installer atomically and teach the old spelling without executing it.
options.code:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
   PASS  100000 cases
$ jet self lsp             # editor argv

$ jet lsp
Error [E2101]: `lsp` moved under `jet self`
 Why: language-server plumbing belongs with Jet's own tooling
 Fix: run `jet self lsp`

options.name: Self group for both
options.detail: Treat fuzzing and LSP as specialist tooling under `jet self`. This makes the flat ring smaller, but separates fuzz from `test` even though both execute test properties and share fixtures.
options.code:
$ jet self fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet self lsp

$ jet fuzz parser.jet
Error [E2101]: `fuzz` moved under `jet self`
 Fix: run `jet self fuzz parser.jet`

options.name: Keep both flat but hide LSP from human help
options.detail: Preserve current argv for integrations and fuzz users. `lsp` is marked machine-facing and omitted from ordinary help/palette unless searched exactly. This avoids a migration but leaves an undocumented top-level exception to the frequency-ring inventory.
options.code:
$ jet fuzz parser.jet --property round_trip
$ jet lsp
# `jet help` omits lsp; `jet ? lsp` still finds it

comparisons.note: Compiler-adjacent protocol servers are commonly launched by editor configuration rather than taught as daily compiler verbs.
Fuzzing stays adjacent to the test/build developer loop even when implemented by specialist machinery.

decisions.title: C-compatible enum layout at the FFI boundary
decisions.gist: Decide whether and how a Jet enum can cross the C boundary. Today every enum at a C signature is rejected (E3203) because no C-safe layout is defined.
decisions.explainer: D-REPRC1 gave structs `#Layout(c)`. Enums have no C layout, so the C ABI stop-line (#436) hard-rejects them. C libraries use enums constantly (status codes, option flags, tagged unions), so the rejection is a real wall. Recommendation A extends the existing `#Layout(c)` mechanism — one layout family, no new sigil — with a beginner-safe default and an expert tag-width override.
decisions.story: Priya binds a C audio library. Its API returns `typedef enum { OK, UNDERRUN, DEVICE_LOST } aud_status;` and takes a configuration union tagged by another enum. In Jet she models both as ordinary enums. The compiler rejects her `#Extern module` signatures with E3203 and offers no path forward — she has to degrade both to raw I32 constants and lose exhaustiveness checking.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: C enum size is formally implementation-defined; payload enums need a tag+union lowering that C callers can actually declare. Patch: fieldless defaults to C `int` width with explicit discriminants required to match the C header's values when nonzero-based; payload enums lower to the well-defined `repr(C)` tag-plus-union form (the layout Rust standardized in RFC 2195); a growable field under `#Layout(c)` stays a compile error exactly like structs (D-REPRC1 family rule).

options.name: #Layout(c) on enums, full — fieldless and payload, expert tag override (recommended)
options.detail: Fieldless enum: C int discriminant, explicit values allowed (`Ok = 0`). Payload enum: repr(C) tag + union lowering, documented byte layout, generated C-side header comment shows the exact struct/union a C caller declares. Expert override `#Layout(c, tag: U8)` pins tag width. One mechanism, same attribute family as structs.

options.name: Fieldless only
options.detail: Fieldless enums get the C int lowering; payload enums stay rejected (E3203) with a fix-it pointing at a hand-written #Layout(c) struct + tag pattern. Covers status codes and flags; tagged unions remain manual.

options.name: Explicit tag always
options.detail: No defaults: every C-boundary enum must state its tag width (`#Layout(c, tag: I32)`). Removes the implementation-defined-int ambiguity entirely, but adds ceremony to the 95% case where C `int` is right.
options.code:
#Layout(c, tag: I32)
enum AudStatus { Ok = 0, Underrun = 1, DeviceLost = 2 }

options.name: Keep rejection
options.detail: Enums never cross the C boundary; users model C enums as Int constants or distinct I32 wrappers. No layout commitment, but every C binding loses exhaustiveness and pattern matching at the seam.
options.code:
// status quo: E3203, bind as
I32 :: aud_poll(dev)

comparisons.note: repr(C) on fieldless enums = C int; repr(C) payload enums have the RFC 2195 defined tag+union layout; repr(u8) etc. pins tag width. Option A mirrors this proven shape.
comparisons.code:
#[repr(C)] enum Status { Ok = 0, Underrun = 1 }
#[repr(C, u8)] enum Packet { Ping(i32), Data(Frame) }

comparisons.note: @objc / C-imported enums carry a fixed raw type; Swift-native enums cannot cross C without one. Same explicit-representation principle.
comparisons.code: enum Status: Int32 { case ok = 0, underrun = 1 }

comparisons.note: enum(u8) pins the tag; extern union + enum tag is the manual tagged-union form. Option C is Zig's always-explicit stance.

decisions.title: REPL persistent history policy
decisions.gist: Choose what the REPL remembers between sessions and how users search or erase it.
decisions.explainer: A gives beginners useful restart continuity while making secret retention explicit and giving experts exact disable, retention, erase, location, permission, and failure controls.
decisions.story: Maya explores a private production incident in Jet, closes her terminal, then returns tomorrow wanting useful commands back without silently retaining secrets forever.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")

options.name: Private persistent default
options.detail: Persist the latest 2,000 successfully parsed submissions per user by default. F3 opens search; `:history search text` is the textual path. `:history clear` erases the whole file. Store at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/jet/repl-history` or the platform state-directory equivalent, owner-only; a corrupt tail is discarded with a warning. All inputs, including effectful or secret-bearing text, are retained because Jet cannot truthfully identify every secret. `JET_REPL_HISTORY=off` disables writes; `JET_REPL_HISTORY_LIMIT=N` changes retention. If storage is unavailable, continue session-only with a visible warning.
options.code:
$ jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
$ jet repl
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
› :history clear
History cleared.

options.name: Session only
options.detail: Retain submissions only in memory until exit. F3 and `:history search text` search this session; `:history clear` clears it. No file, environment override, or restart recovery exists.
options.code:
$ jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
$ jet repl
› :history search deploy
No history matches.

options.name: Opt-in persistence
options.detail: Default to session-only history. `JET_REPL_HISTORY=on` stores the latest 2,000 successfully parsed submissions at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/jet/repl-history` or the platform state-directory equivalent, owner-only. F3 and `:history search text` search it; `:history clear` erases the whole file; `JET_REPL_HISTORY_LIMIT=N` changes retention. All inputs, including effectful or secret-bearing text, persist. A corrupt tail is discarded with a warning; unavailable storage falls back visibly to session-only.
options.code:
$ JET_REPL_HISTORY=on jet repl
› deploy_preview(region: "us-east")
Preview ready.
$ JET_REPL_HISTORY=on jet repl
› :history search deploy
deploy_preview(region: "us-east")

comparisons.note: Interactive history is commonly persisted through readline configuration and searched interactively.
History persists automatically and exposes explicit search and deletion controls.

decisions.title: REPL multiline editing keys
decisions.gist: Choose how raw-terminal users edit and submit a multiline REPL entry.
decisions.explainer: A preserves instant one-line use, derives the default from Jet syntax instead of modes, and retains explicit expert controls for forced newline and submission.
decisions.story: Iris writes a small function directly at the prompt. She needs ordinary Enter behavior for quick expressions and a predictable way to edit and submit several lines without accidental execution.

options.name: Syntax-aware Enter
options.detail: In raw mode, Enter submits complete input and inserts a newline when the parser says input is incomplete. Alt-Enter, encoded portably as Escape then Enter, always inserts a newline. A blank Enter on an empty continuation line force-submits. One-line Enter remains unchanged; cooked/non-TTY mode keeps today's balance-based continuation.

options.name: Blank line submits blocks
options.detail: One-line Enter still submits. Once Enter encounters incomplete syntax, raw mode enters block editing: later Enter inserts lines even after syntax becomes complete, and an empty line submits the block. Escape then Enter inserts a newline without submitting. Cooked/non-TTY mode keeps today's balance-based continuation.

options.name: Explicit edit mode
options.detail: One-line Enter still submits. F4 opens a multiline editor for the current entry; Enter inserts lines and F4 submits. `:edit` opens it and a `:submit` control line submits without becoming Jet source. Cooked/non-TTY mode keeps today's balance-based continuation.
options.code:
› :edit
· fn total(xs: [Int]) -> Int {
·     return xs.sum()
· }
· :submit
› total([3, 4, 5])
12 : Int

comparisons.note: Syntax completeness starts continuation and a blank line finishes a block.
Enter submits while an alternate Enter chord inserts another line.
comparisons.code:
> const total = (xs) =>
    xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)

decisions.title: REPL Ctrl-C during evaluation
decisions.gist: Choose what Ctrl-C does while submitted Jet code is still running.
decisions.explainer: A matches beginner expectations, preserves truthful prior state, and tells experts exactly which external effects cannot be rolled back while keeping interrupted work addressable.
decisions.story: Noah accidentally starts an endless calculation in the REPL. He presses Ctrl-C expecting immediate recovery without losing useful state created before that turn.
decisions.inWild:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back.
› saved_result
42

options.name: Interrupt turn, keep session
options.detail: Poll cancellation at every interpreter instruction and before and after each runtime call; Jet-controlled execution must restore the terminal and prompt within 100 ms of Ctrl-C. A blocking external call follows that call's cancellation contract and the UI says when it is still stopping. Keep prior session state and commit no bindings from the interrupted turn. External I/O already performed remains and the message says so. Record the turn as interrupted and allow rerun. Outside evaluation, the existing ruling remains: Ctrl-C clears a nonempty line first; Ctrl-C at an empty prompt exits.
options.code:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back.
› saved_result
42

options.name: Interrupt and restart session
options.detail: Poll cancellation at every interpreter instruction and before and after each runtime call; Jet-controlled execution must restore the terminal within 100 ms of Ctrl-C. A blocking external call follows that call's cancellation contract and the UI says when it is still stopping. Then discard every REPL binding and start a fresh session. External I/O already performed remains and the message says so. Keep the interrupted turn only in history, not as rerunnable live state. Outside evaluation, existing line-clear and empty-prompt exit behavior remains.
options.code:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back. Session restarted with no bindings.
›

options.name: Exit REPL
options.detail: Poll cancellation at every interpreter instruction and before and after each runtime call; Jet-controlled execution must restore terminal state and exit within 100 ms of Ctrl-C. A blocking external call follows that call's cancellation contract and the UI says when it is still stopping. External I/O already performed remains and the message says so. Outside evaluation, existing line-clear and empty-prompt exit behavior remains.
options.code:
› loop { compute() }
^C
Interrupted. External effects already performed were not rolled back.
$

comparisons.note: Ctrl-C raises KeyboardInterrupt and normally returns to the same interactive session.
Ctrl-C interrupts current execution and returns to the prompt; repeated Ctrl-C exits.

decisions.comment: While running interrupt turn but when no turn is running it should exit. If a turn is running in repl, pressing ctrl c twice should exit repl, once to interrupt, the second to exit

decisions.title: Batch semantic codemod object law
decisions.gist: Choose how one replayable codemod object expresses ordered semantic rewrites across examples and UI fixtures.
decisions.explainer: D-CODEMOD1 remains the one engine. `jet codemod dry-run|apply|undo` and existing v1 objects/logs stay valid. A missing `version`, or `version: 1`, with `{entry, operation: "rename", from, to}` lowers internally to one `symbol_rename` rule and keeps today's entry-closure scope and output compatibility. Existing v1 logs remain readable; new logs carry `schema: 2` but undo lowers both schemas to the same verified inverse plan. A v2 object lowers to the same TextEdit plan, journal, log, and undo model; no second executor exists. A v2 object requires `project`, resolved relative to the object file, and `roots`. The canonical project path owns `.jet/codemods/<sanitized-name>.log.json`, `.lock`, and any recovery journal. For card #451, each root names either one regular `.jet` file or a directory, and must canonicalize beneath `<project>/examples` or `<project>/tests/ui`; `..`, absolute escape, and symlink escape fail. Directory discovery recursively sorts regular `.jet` files by project-relative byte path; a file root discovers only that file. Each discovered file is an entry compilation unit; its transitive Jet imports join that unit. The same physical file imported by several entries is indexed and edited once. Imports outside editable roots may be read for parsing, name resolution, and semantic identity but never edited; a rule selecting one fails with its path. Non-Jet files are ignored except the exact paired `tests/ui/<name>.stderr` of a touched UI fixture and declared snapshot inputs. Every rule resolves against the currently staged tree after prior rules. Within each compilation unit, every bare identifier in a match template resolves through semindex at the candidate node; that resolved definition anchor, not spelling, controls the match. Every non-capture identifier introduced by a replacement template must resolve uniquely in that same staged compilation unit before an edit is accepted. A rename destination is checked in every affected definition/reference scope and fails on collision or changed binding. A semantic symbol anchor is `(canonical definition module path, symbol kind, current definition span)`; references bind to that anchor through semindex. Independent same-spelled definitions remain independent anchors; selectors either match all and assert the total or narrow with `defined_in`. If a match source or destination resolves to zero or multiple definitions in any unit, the rule fails with unit path and candidates. Rules run in listed order. Within one rule, overlapping/nested edits fail; overlap across rules is intentional sequencing because rule N sees reindexed output from rule N-1. Duplicate ids, unknown fields, ambiguous anchors, unused captures, invalid replacement nodes, and zero matches unless `allow_zero: true` fail. Validation is transactional data, not a code-only check: a `clean` root must finish with zero lexer/parser/sema diagnostics; every touched `fixture` `.jet` must render a complete stderr snapshot. Without `snapshot_after`, generated stderr must equal the existing paired `.stderr` byte-for-byte. With `snapshot_after`, each value is a project-relative path resolved beneath the canonical project; every component must be non-symlink and the final input must be a regular file. Absolute paths, `..`, project escape, symlink, directory, and aliasing the destination `.stderr` fail. That file contains the complete replacement bytes; generated stderr must equal it byte-for-byte, and the paired `.stderr` becomes a planned edit shown in dry-run and committed/undone with source. Dry-run and apply take the exclusive codemod lock before discovery and hold it through discovery, indexing, every staged rule, validation, diagnostic rendering, final hash verification, and output/commit. The lock coordinates codemod processes only; ordinary editors need not honor it. Therefore the engine fingerprints every discovered source, read-only import, existing `.stderr`, and `snapshot_after` input on first read, rehashes all of them after rendering, and refuses with exact drift paths before printing a ready plan or writing anything if any changed. Apply rechecks every destination immediately before its rename and refuses observed drift. This does not close the check-to-rename race with a noncooperating editor: only codemod peers honor the lock, so an editor can still write after the check and be overwritten by the rename. Apply prints that limitation before confirmation; `--yes` accepts it. It writes same-directory temp files, fsyncs file contents, writes+fsyncs a journal containing transaction id, state, every before/after hash, complete before bytes, temp path, and destination, then fsyncs parent directories. Commit uses sequential same-filesystem renames; it is recoverable, not falsely advertised as globally atomic or safe from noncooperating concurrent writers. After each rename it advances and fsyncs journal state. On write/rename/fsync failure, rollback restores a destination only when its current hash equals the transaction's recorded after-hash; any other hash may be an unseen concurrent write, so recovery preserves that destination and the journal, reports the conflict, and refuses further codemod work. A crash leaves the journal. Before any later dry-run/apply/undo, the engine locks and recovers: hashes matching all after states complete the log; mixed/before states attempt the same conditional rollback, restoring only destinations still at recorded transaction hashes. Ambiguous drift or failed recovery preserves the journal, changes nothing further, prints exact paths/hashes, and refuses all codemod work until recovery can succeed. Only successful completion writes+fsyncs the schema-2 replay log and removes+fsyncs the journal. Undo first locks and verifies every current after-hash, then uses the identical temp/journal/fsync/recovery protocol to restore byte-exact before content, including `.stderr`; any mismatch causes zero writes. Dry-run writes no source, snapshot, log, temp, or new journal; after the final stable-snapshot rehash it prints path-ordered rule counts, validation, and unified source+snapshot diffs while still holding the lock.
decisions.story: Maya must update a helper across runnable examples and diagnostic fixtures. One rule renames a semantic function; another changes a call shape while preserving its argument. She needs one reviewed plan where code and every affected UI snapshot move together. Dev needs deterministic discovery, stable symbol identity, exact match counts, crash recovery, and byte-exact undo before approving the apply.

options.name: Typed AST templates
options.detail: Rules are `symbol_rename` or `ast_rewrite`. An AST rule declares `node` as `expr`, `stmt`, `item`, or `type`; `match` and `replace` are current Jet source parsed in that node class. `$name` captures exactly one subtree. `$args...` captures an ordered zero-or-more sequence only where that node grammar has a list. A repeated scalar capture requires structural equality. Bare identifiers, labels, literals, operators, and syntax match exactly after semantic name resolution; comments and layout do not participate. Replacement uses only declared captures, preserves captured bytes when safe, and otherwise formats the replacement node with `jet fmt`; variadic captures splice only into the same list kind. Every root declares `clean` or `fixture`. `clean` requires zero lexer/parser/sema diagnostics after every rule. `fixture` requires the generated final diagnostic output to equal the paired `.stderr` byte-for-byte. If expected output intentionally changes, `snapshot_after` maps the `.jet` path to a repository file containing the complete new `.stderr`; dry-run compares generated bytes to it and shows the paired `.stderr` diff, while apply writes those exact verified bytes in the same transaction. A code-only apply is impossible. Recommended: Jet-shaped patterns are readable to beginners; node classes, semantic anchors, captures, exact counts, and snapshots give experts precise control without regex.

options.name: Finite semantic operations
options.detail: Rules choose a closed registry: `symbol_rename`, `call_rename`, `call_add_named_arg`, `import_move`, or `marker_replace`. `symbol_rename` takes a semantic selector and identifier. `call_rename` changes only calls resolved to the selected function. `call_add_named_arg` parses `value` as one Jet expression, rejects an existing or positionally conflicting label, and inserts through the AST argument list. `import_move` takes exact resolved `from` and `to` module paths and preserves the local alias. `marker_replace` takes exact current PascalCase marker names, changes the marker AST node only, and rejects different argument arity; it does not text-replace comments or strings. No interpolation exists in B. Unknown operations/fields fail. Roots, anchors, ordering, exact `matches`, validation, full snapshot pairing, recoverable transaction, log, and undo are identical to the shared law. This is easiest to discover and audit, but a new migration shape requires a future ratified registry entry.

options.name: Semantic selectors and typed edits
options.detail: Each rule has `select` plus `edit`. Selectors allow only `node`, `symbol_kind`, `resolved_name`, `defined_in`, `called_from`, and exact `argument_count`; globs are project-relative and may narrow but never widen roots. Edits are `rename_symbol`, `replace_callee`, `insert_named_arg`, or `replace_node`. `replace_node.source` is parsed as the selected node class. It may interpolate `$argument[N]`, `$receiver`, or `$node`; indices are zero-based, each placeholder expands to that captured AST subtree, and no other `$` form exists. A missing/out-of-range placeholder, wrong node class, label collision, or marker/value parse error fails. Marker edits use `node: "marker"`, exact PascalCase `resolved_name`, and a complete replacement marker source such as `#New(arg)`; arguments are never implicitly copied. Roots, anchors, ordering, exact counts, validation, full snapshot pairing, journal, log, and undo follow the shared law. This gives experts strongest targeting, but simple work requires learning selector/edit vocabulary.

comparisons.note: Structural templates with holes stay readable across formatting. Option A adds Jet node classes and semantic resolution.
Semantic matchers separate identity from edits. Option C adopts that precision with a deliberately small selector set.
Compiler facts produce checked edits and conflicts stop the run. Jet adds ordered multi-rule objects, paired diagnostic snapshots, and recoverable replay logs.

decisions.title: Generic-module value parameter domain and evaluation
decisions.gist: Choose which compile-time values may specialize a generic module and where those values may be used.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified floor. D-GENMOD1=A approves modules parameterized by types and values. D-GENMOD2=A fixes one `<...>` list, annotation-kind classification, and mirrored instantiation such as `module StringCache32 = Lru<String, 32>`. It supersedes D-GENMOD1's prototype parentheses. S26 otherwise says comptime is value-only and never parameterizes/selects types; every option below states whether generic-module parameters create a narrow exception. No option adds a keyword or second generic syntax. `D-GENMOD-IDENTITY1` and `D-GENMOD-BODY1` are proposed companion ballot IDs only: neither is live, queued, nor ratified. The ballots may be presented and ratified in any order, but their implementation dependencies are directional. VALUE1 alone owns value domain, evaluation, substitution/use positions, and canonical value bytes. IDENTITY1 may define its structural choice independently but cannot consume/finalize value-argument identity until VALUE1 ratifies. BODY1 may define declaration/capture law independently, but every selected body feature that reads a value parameter waits for VALUE1. Cross-alias semantic/code/cache dedup waits for IDENTITY1. Nominal struct/enum member emission waits for BODY1 only when its selected option admits those declarations. Type-only/function-only generic-module work need not wait on irrelevant companion outcomes.

Shared resolution law. Parser stores each declaration annotation and alias argument as unresolved syntax with exact spans; casing never determines kind. A bare parameter such as `T` is a type parameter. For `name: Annotation`, sema resolves Annotation in the declaration's lexical scope: a trait/bound makes a type parameter, while an allowed concrete value type makes a value parameter. Unknown, ambiguous, or disallowed annotations reject at the annotation. Once target template resolves, each alias argument is parsed/contextualized by its parameter slot: type slots require a type; value slots accept one ordinary expression delimited by the top-level comma or closing `>`, with nested calls/operators/collections using normal expression grammar. Thus `Ring<Packet, 32 + 32, true>` is unambiguous without uppercase/lowercase guessing. Parameter names still obey D-CASING1 style diagnostics, but spelling never changes semantics. No defaults, named arguments, inference, packs, implicit conversions, or module-valued parameters are introduced.

Option A exact domain. Value parameter annotations are Bool, Int, Char, String, or a named fieldless enum. Int is Jet's checked i64; overflow is a compile-time error. Char is one Unicode scalar. String is its exact UTF-8 scalar sequence; no NFC/case/path normalization occurs. A fieldless enum value includes its resolved nominal type and variant. Float is forbidden because NaN payloads and signed zero defeat obvious equality; lists/maps/structs/payload enums/options/results/functions/types/modules/handles/raw pointers/shared state are forbidden because they introduce mutability, ownership, allocation graphs, or open identity rules. Future additions require another decision.

Option A expression/effect law. An argument must type-check as its annotation and evaluate completely through the existing fuel-limited comptime interpreter before generic-module expansion. Allowed expressions are literals; enum cases; arithmetic, comparison, Boolean, string, and `if` expressions; references to earlier immutable `const`/`comptime` bindings; and calls whose entire reached graph is accepted by Tier-0 pure comptime law. Runtime bindings, ambient state, mutation, task/process/network/time/random access, `#Impure`, Tier-1/Tier-2 effects, `find`, `fetch`, `embed_file`, `embed_bytes`, reflection, panic, fuel exhaustion, division by zero, overflow, and a non-value result reject. Arguments cannot reference the template's parameters, sibling arguments, or declarations inside the uninstantiated template. Evaluation order is source order for diagnostics only; values have no side effects. Existing comptime failures keep their existing exact diagnostic codes; generic-slot type/kind failures use the codes below.

Option A binding/use law and exact amendments. After all arguments validate, sema clones the template and binds each evaluated result as an immutable comptime constant before checking any cloned item. It may appear wherever an ordinary constant of that type is already legal in function bodies, const initializers, array/index/range expressions, `comptime if`, marker value arguments, and nested declarations later admitted by BODY1. It cannot set enum discriminants: Jet has no ratified user-facing enum-discriminant law. It cannot construct an identifier, module/import path, field name, marker name, trait name, type argument, overload set, or dispatch target. Option A and C atomically amend both S26 and S76/D-FIXARR1: today `[T#N]` has a compile-time length but no general named-value const-generic surface; inside a generic-module specialization only, `[T#capacity]` becomes legal when capacity is an Int value parameter, evaluates before body checking, and must satisfy every existing fixed-list range/layout/overflow rule. This is a new narrow named-value use of the S76 spelling, not merely use of an already-open slot. No other type position accepts a value expression; no general const generics, comptime-created types, or type-returning computation becomes legal. Proposed BODY1 decides which declaration kinds may contain these substitutions; any BODY1-selected value-using feature activates only after VALUE1, while nominal identity/dedup separately waits for IDENTITY1 where relevant.

Option A normalization/equality and identity contribution. Evaluation produces one typed GenModuleValue. Bool canonical bytes are domain byte 0x01 plus 0x00/0x01. Int is domain 0x02 plus its signed i64 two's-complement eight-byte big-endian form. Char is domain 0x03 plus its Unicode scalar as four-byte big-endian u32. String is domain 0x04 plus u64-BE UTF-8 byte length and exact UTF-8 bytes. Enum is domain 0x05 plus u64-length-framed resolved package/module/type identity and u64-length-framed variant name. Every field is length-framed where variable; concatenation is ordered by declared parameter position. Two value arguments are equal exactly when their resolved annotation type and Jet value are equal; equal values have identical canonical bytes, unequal values do not. Constant spelling, source path/span, binding name, expression tree, and evaluation route are absent. These bytes are the sole value-argument contribution. Proposed, not-live IDENTITY1 may be decided in any order but may consume/finalize these bytes only after VALUE1 ratifies; this ballot does not decide applicative versus generative module/type identity.

Diagnostics/I4. E0853 remains `generic module argument <N> for <Template> has type <got>, but value parameter <name> needs <want>`; Why says the resolved slot is a value parameter and no implicit conversion occurs; Fix supplies an expression of <want> or changes the declaration. Reserve E0856 for `generic module value parameter <name> cannot use type <type>`; Why lists the selected option's closed domain and identity reason; Fix chooses an allowed type or a type parameter. Reserve E0857 for `generic module argument <N> for <Template> is not a compile-time value`; Why names the first runtime/effect/non-value dependency; Fix passes a literal/immutable Tier-0 value or moves work inside the module. Existing overflow/panic/fuel diagnostics remain canonical but point through a related note to alias argument and parameter declaration. Each emitted code needs diagnostics.md What/Why/Fix, tests/ui source+snapshot, `jet explain`, and AOT/comptime parity tests before shipping.

Beginner pass: literal Int/Bool arguments work like ordinary generic arguments; values become read-only names inside the module. Expert pass: exact evaluation tier, allowed layout slot, canonical bytes, nominal enum identity, errors, and identity handoff are reproducible. Hybrid pass: literals and computed pure constants use one sema/interpreter path; no beginner facade or separate template engine exists.
decisions.story: Priya publishes one ring-buffer module for embedded targets. Capacity changes storage layout, while a checked flag removes bounds-check branches in trusted builds. She wants `Ring<Packet, 64, true>` to produce one ordinary module whose types, constants, and functions all agree on those values. She also needs two imports of the same arguments to mean the same specialization, not two subtly different buffers.

options.name: Closed immutable values plus layout slots
options.detail: Recommended. Bool/Int/Char/String/fieldless-enum values evaluate under Tier-0 comptime and bind as immutable constants. Int additionally enables the narrowly amended `[T#capacity]` generic-module form under S26 + S76/D-FIXARR1. Gives the ratified feature real value specialization while keeping identity closed, safe, deterministic, and explicit.

options.name: Values may affect expressions only
options.detail: Use the same closed types, evaluation, normalization, and diagnostics as A, but preserve S26 literally: parameters may appear in runtime/const expressions and comptime branches, never `[T#N]`, layout, types, or dispatch. Avoids a new type-level exception, but `capacity` cannot define the ring buffer's storage type, so true fixed-size generic modules remain impossible.

options.name: Int-only layout parameters
options.detail: Allow only Int, evaluated under the same Tier-0 law, in ordinary Int expressions and the same narrow S26 + S76/D-FIXARR1 `[T#capacity]` amendment as A. Covers capacities and dimensions with the smallest identity domain, but forces separate modules or type parameters for Boolean modes, string protocol labels, and enum policies despite those values already being safe comptime data.

comparisons.note: Rust permits a restricted structural const domain and uses evaluated values in type identity/layout. A adopts the closed/reproducible part without adding a general const-generic system outside generic modules.
comparisons.code: struct Ring<T, const N: usize> { slots: [T; N] }

comparisons.note: Zig accepts broad comptime values and types. Jet keeps one smaller closed value domain and forbids type-valued computation, ambient evaluation, and arbitrary structural identity.
comparisons.code: fn Ring(comptime T: type, comptime n: usize) type { ... }

comparisons.note: Functor arguments are modules, not scalar values. Jet's ratified type/value module parameters target direct configuration while module-valued parameters remain out of scope.

decisions.title: What declarations and captures belong inside a generic module?
decisions.gist: Choose whether a specialized generic module has the full body and lexical scope of an ordinary module.
decisions.explainer:
D-GENMOD1=A already says instantiation yields a specialized normal module. D-GENMOD2=A fixes unified `<...>` parameters and alias instantiation. BODY1 decides only body item admission, definition-site capture, visibility/coherence consequences, and nested-template cycle lookup. It does not decide value evaluation/normalization/substitution or specialization identity/dedup/fingerprints.

Exact item matrix. A and B admit functions; structs; enums; tags; runtime `const`; `comptime` constants; traits; ordinary trait impls; error-conversion impls; OS-gated impls; tests; benches; ordinary nested modules; nested generic-module templates; and nested module aliases. Existing legal function/type/item markers remain legal only on their existing declaration kinds and keep current semantics; markers are not new items. Tests/benches instantiate only in their existing build modes. C admits functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime `const`, `comptime` constants, and existing legal markers on those admitted declarations. C rejects traits, every impl/error-conversion form, OS-gated impls, tests, benches, ordinary nested modules, nested generic modules, and nested aliases. Every option rejects inline `use`/`pub use` until ordinary module law admits it, plus file/package/build/FFI/C-module/generated-binding/role-module/policy/protocol/state/migration/user-derive/generic-package declarations; those retain their existing homes.

Capture law is independent of argument-value law. Under A/C, non-parameter names resolve in the template definition scope, never alias scope. Under B, only parameters, template-local declarations, and ordinary Core/prelude are visible. Parameters shadow outer names; duplicates use ordinary diagnostics. Public specialized APIs cannot expose private captured declarations. Live open D-GENMOD-VALUE1 owns value evaluation and use; BODY1 does not pre-decide it.

Ordinary orphan law checks expanded declarations: supplied/captured external type and trait remain external, so instantiation never grants an external-for-external impl. Proposed, not-live D-GENMOD-IDENTITY1 gates nominal emission/equality for every specialized struct, enum, tag, and template-declared trait. It also gates whether aliases share a specialization; duplicate nominal declarations; duplicate/coherent trait and error-conversion impls; and semantic/code/cache dedup. BODY1 selects whether these items belong, but they cannot emit until IDENTITY1 ratifies. Functions and constants have no nominal-identity dependency.

Lookup is order-independent: visible top-level/nested templates and aliases may refer forward or backward. Sema collects declarations, builds one dependency graph, then expands in deterministic topological order. Direct/indirect cycles are E0855 at the triggering alias with the full alias/template chain. Source order breaks only diagnostic-order ties, never legality. No expand-until-stable loop. Admitted output enters ordinary sema before codegen.

Dependencies are conditional. VALUE1 is live/open; its selected value behavior remains unresolved. IDENTITY1 is proposed/not live. BODY1 may ratify the matrix and implement function/constant admission, capture/visibility checks, and E0855 independently. Any selected value-using feature waits for VALUE1. Specialized nominal emission/equality, duplicate/coherent impl handling, and cross-alias dedup wait for IDENTITY1.

Diagnostics. E0854 is item-set-only: `generic module <Template> contains a <kind> item, which is not allowed`; Why names the selected closed set; Fix moves it to ordinary module scope or uses an admitted kind. An admitted kind retires its E0854 path; the old snapshot becomes a positive migration test. Reserve E0858 for sealed capture: `generic module <Template> captures <name> from its definition scope`. Why names B's parameter/local/Core-only scope. Fix is per kind and never assumes a value-parameter domain: type -> add a type parameter; trait -> add it as a bound on a type parameter; function -> move/localize helper inside; module -> move needed helpers inside or expose operations through a type parameter trait bound; constant/value -> define it from template-local/Core inputs inside or move the dependent declaration outside. E0858 needs diagnostics.md, `jet explain`, canonical source+snapshot fixtures for value/type/trait/function/module captures, and compiling fixes. E0855 needs its full-chain snapshot.

Beginner: one ordinary-looking parameterized module, private by default. Expert: exact matrix, scope, visibility, orphan, dependencies, and cycle graph. Hybrid: one module mechanism; no template sublanguage or AST/text injection.
decisions.story: Priya maintains a storage library with one key type, one shard count, an Entry type, a Codec trait implementation, constants, and helper submodules that must stay synchronized. She wants to instantiate that family once for production and once for tests. The decision determines whether the family can remain one coherent module, which surrounding names it may use, and whether specialization can accidentally gain authority or violate trait ownership.

options.name: Full ordinary-module parity with lexical capture
options.detail: Recommended. Admits functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime/comptime constants, traits, trait/error-conversion/OS-gated impls, tests, benches, ordinary nested modules, nested generic modules, aliases, and existing legal markers. Uses definition-site lexical capture. Nominal emission and coherent duplicate impl behavior remain gated on IDENTITY1.

options.name: Full declarations, sealed parameter-only scope
options.detail: Admits the same complete item/marker set as A: functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime/comptime constants, traits, all ordinary impl forms including OS-gated, tests, benches, ordinary/nested generic modules, and aliases. Seals scope to parameters, locals, and Core/prelude. Nominal/impl identity still waits for IDENTITY1.

options.name: Data-and-function capsule only
options.detail: Admits only functions, structs, enums, tags, runtime `const`, `comptime` constants, and existing legal markers on those kinds, with definition-site lexical capture. Rejects traits, trait/error-conversion/OS-gated impls, tests, benches, ordinary nested modules, nested generic modules, and aliases via item-set-only E0854. Nominal struct/enum/tag emission still waits for IDENTITY1.

comparisons.note: A functor body is a full module expression: it may define types, values, nested modules, and module relationships. Inputs are explicit module parameters, while ordinary lexical scope remains available.
comparisons.code:
module Make (Key : ORDERED) = struct
  type t = (Key.t * string) list
  module Index = Map.Make(Key)
  let empty = []
end

comparisons.note: Templates can generate types, constants, functions, and nested declarations, but dependent lookup and specialization rules are a major source of surprise. Jet avoids textual substitution and checks one specialized ordinary module in sema.

Rust has no generic modules. Related generic types, traits, impls, and constants stay at module scope, so a family cannot be instantiated and named as one namespace. Jet generic modules exist specifically to preserve that family boundary.

A comptime function can return a type namespace containing declarations and capture parameters. It is powerful, but folds module generation into general compile-time execution; Jet keeps a declarative module mechanism checked by ordinary sema.

decisions.title: Generic-module instantiation and nominal type identity
decisions.gist: Choose whether repeating the same generic-module application means the same module and the same exported nominal types.
decisions.explainer:
Ratified D-GENMOD1=A makes a parameterized module instantiate to a specialized normal module. Ratified D-GENMOD2=A fixes one unified `<...>` parameter/argument list: parameter annotation kind alone distinguishes type from value parameters; casing is style-only and never identity or semantic classification. This ballot does not reopen that syntax. It closes the missing semantic law: whether module application is applicative (same template and arguments imply one instance) or generative (each alias declaration creates a fresh instance), and therefore what identity exported nominal structs/enums carry.

Current truth is only an MVP. `expand_generic_module_aliases` clones functions into a `CodeModule` named after each alias, substitutes type parameters in function signatures only, and erases templates/aliases before registration. Value arguments, bounds, cycles, body references, exported structs/enums/constants, cross-file templates, JIT parity, stable fingerprints, cache reuse, and semantic-index projection remain staged. Codegen names follow the alias, so two aliases of the same application do not yet have a canonical shared identity or dedup law. D-TYPEALIAS1 remains separate: `alias X = Y` is transparent type naming; `module X = Template<...>` instantiates a module and must not become a disguised second type-alias mechanism.

Exact byte and companion law. frame(B) is unsigned u64 big-endian byte length followed by B. text(S) is frame(exact UTF-8 bytes); no extra Unicode, path, or case normalization occurs. `hex64(H)` rejects anything except 64 lowercase hexadecimal ASCII characters and contributes the decoded 32 bytes; every fingerprint output is exactly 64 lowercase hexadecimal ASCII characters. ResolvedPackageBytes is `text("jet.package.v1") || text(resolved package name) || text(canonical SemVer) || frame(LockedSourceIdentityBytes)`. LockedSourceIdentityBytes is stable and closed: workspace = `text("workspace") || text(workspace identity declared by the resolved workspace graph) || text(package-root WorkspacePath)`; registry = `text("registry") || text(canonical HTTPS registry authority/index identity from the lock resolver) || text(package name) || text(canonical SemVer)`; git = `text("git") || text(canonical credential-free repository identity from the lock resolver) || frame(exact decoded revision object id)`; path = `text("path") || text(locked workspace-relative dependency root) || text(resolved dependency package name) || text(canonical SemVer)`. Whole-tree, file-content, lockfile-content, body-semantic, and interface hashes never enter package/definition/type identity; they belong only to cache invalidation and API compatibility facts. Canonical repository/registry identities are the lockfile's single source keys: lowercase IDNA host, explicit nondefault port only, normalized absolute slash path, uppercase percent escapes, no credentials/query/fragment/dot segments; git ssh/scp spellings normalize to that same credential-free identity before lock write. DefinitionFullKey is text("jet.genmod.definition.v1") plus frame(ResolvedPackageBytes), text(defining WorkspacePath), each framed lexical module segment, text("generic-module"), and text(template name). DefinitionId is lowercase Hex64 SHA-256(DefinitionFullKey). Every store persists schema, id, and full_key and byte-compares full_key on hits; same id with different bytes is ICE 101. No truncation, display name, span, absolute path, import alias, Rust name, map order, or compile order participates.

Type arguments contribute frame(canonical sema TypeFullKey) after transparent aliases resolve. Live open D-GENMOD-VALUE1 exclusively owns value domain, evaluation, selected canonical bytes, and E0853/E0856/E0857. IDENTITY1 may ratify first, but no value-bearing identity ships until VALUE1 ratifies; afterward it consumes exactly VALUE1's selected bytes with no second normalization. `count(N)` is unsigned u64 big-endian. ParameterBytes begins with count(parameter count). Each type parameter is byte 0x01, text(name), byte 0x00 for no bound or byte 0x01 plus frame(resolved trait DefinitionFullKey) for a bound. Each value parameter is byte 0x02, text(name), and frame(annotation TypeFullKey); annotation absence is impossible and rejects before identity. ArgumentBytes begins with count(argument count); each type argument is byte 0x01 plus frame(TypeFullKey), each value argument byte 0x02 plus frame(the complete VALUE1-selected byte string). ApplicationFullKey is `text("jet.genmod.application.v1") || frame(DefinitionFullKey) || frame(ParameterBytes) || frame(ArgumentBytes)`. Counts, kind bytes, names, bound presence, resolved trait identities, and value annotations therefore cannot collide. ApplicationFingerprint is SHA-256(ApplicationFullKey). Under A, InstanceFullKey equals ApplicationFullKey. Under B, InstanceFullKey is text("jet.genmod.instance.v1") plus frame(ApplicationFullKey) and frame(AliasDeclarationFullKey), where the alias key uses the same package/workspace/module/kind/name fields with kind "module-instantiation-alias". InstanceFingerprint is lowercase Hex64 SHA-256(InstanceFullKey). Under C, PackageSealedInstanceFullKey is text("jet.genmod.package-instance.v1") || frame(ApplicationFullKey) || frame(the consuming package's ResolvedPackageBytes). PackageSealedInstanceFingerprint is lowercase Hex64 SHA-256(PackageSealedInstanceFullKey). Every package-sealed store persists (schema, id, full_key), byte-compares PackageSealedInstanceFullKey on every fingerprint hit, and reports ICE 101 if one fingerprint maps to different full-key bytes.

Nominal member identity is conditional on live open D-GENMOD-BODY1. Until BODY1 ratifies an option admitting structs/enums/tags/traits, E0854 remains and no member TypeFullKey exists. After admission, all options preserve Jet's S28 nominal law; no struct, enum, tag, or trait becomes structurally equal by shape. MemberKind is 0x01 struct, 0x02 enum, 0x03 Jet tag, or 0x04 trait; MemberGenericBytes is count(argument count), then each type argument as 0x01||frame(TypeFullKey) and each value argument as 0x02||frame(exact VALUE1 bytes). NominalMemberFullKey is text("jet.genmod.member-type.v1") || frame(option identity basis) || byte(MemberKind) || count(lexical member path segment count) || each text(segment) || text(declared name) || frame(MemberGenericBytes). A's identity basis is ApplicationFullKey; B's is alias-generative InstanceFullKey; C's is PackageSealedInstanceFullKey. TypeFingerprint is SHA-256(NominalMemberFullKey). Trait associated items/signatures, tag qualification, struct fields/layout, and enum variants affect interface/body/cache compatibility but never replace declaration identity with structural equality. An impl mints no type identity: coherence keys on instantiated nominal trait TypeFullKey and target TypeFullKey and applies ordinary orphan/duplicate law. Qualified types preserve written tag order through the existing qualifier TypeFullKey law. Every id collision compares the exact full key.

Cross-file/package law. Loader resolves a template to one DefinitionId before instantiation; re-export/import paths never mint identity. Dependency package identity comes from the resolved package/version/source identity already used by the module graph, so two physical copies of the same resolved package object share and two distinct resolved package versions/sources do not. Private instances deduplicate within the loaded package graph under the chosen option. Public exported types persist their TypeFingerprint into semantic index, interface/API facts, and cache artifacts; readers reject unknown schema or mismatched full keys instead of guessing. Cycles are detected on the active full instance key before body checking and report the complete source-level application chain.

Codegen/cache/LSP law. Sema owns instantiation, bounds, value checking, cycles, privacy, and nominal equality before TIR (I3). Each reachable semantic instance is checked once per canonical identity, lowered once, and codegen emits one specialization per canonical code key; aliases become source-name projections only. If an option makes two nominal instances distinct but their executable bodies safely share, code dedup may use ApplicationFingerprint plus a checked template-body semantic hash only after sema type-erases the distinction; it never changes type equality. Incremental cache keys include compiler ABI/schema, DefinitionId, normalized arguments, checked template-body semantic hash, target/profile/effects/layout inputs, and dependency interface fingerprints. Alias renames invalidate only name/reference projections under A; under B it intentionally creates a new generative InstanceFingerprint and invalidates that alias instance's semantic/type projections; under C, alias rename, import rename, and re-export within the same consuming package preserve PackageSealedInstanceFingerprint; changing the consuming package's resolved source, name, or version changes it. C's semantic, nominal-type, public-interface, and LSP keys use PackageSealedInstanceFingerprint, while checked executable/template-body caches may reuse ApplicationFingerprint across package seals without making types equal. The semantic index records definition, instantiation, alias, argument, exported-member, references, and chosen identity relation; go-to-definition from an alias reaches both alias and template application, find-references joins all aliases only when the chosen option says they share; under C it joins aliases within one consuming package and keeps references from different consuming packages distinct. AOT/JIT/dev/comptime use the same checked instances and cache law.

Diagnostics. E0850/E0851 remain unknown-template/arity and E0852 remains unsatisfied bound. VALUE1 alone defines and imports E0853/E0856/E0857 byte-for-byte; IDENTITY1 neither restates nor widens them. E0854 remains BODY1's staged/item-set error until its selected option admits the relevant member kind. E0855 What is `generic module instantiation forms a cycle`; Why prints the full alias/template/argument chain; Fix names the application edge to remove or replace. E0859 is identity-only: What `generic module identity collided`; Why says two distinct full keys produced one fingerprint; Fix says `report this internal compiler error`; the process exits 101 and never falls back. VALUE1 retains E0853/E0856/E0857 unchanged. Ordinary mismatch between distinct nominal exported types uses the existing type-mismatch diagnostic, but names both fully qualified instance applications and explains whether different arguments or the selected generative rule made them distinct. Every new/changed code needs diagnostics.md What/Why/Fix, UI source, exact snapshot, JSON/LSP parity, and `jet explain` before emission (I4).

Beginner pass: write one module application anywhere; identical applications either work together by the stated rule or produce an error naming both source spellings and why. No fingerprint/cache vocabulary appears in ordinary diagnostics. Expert pass: package/version identity, canonical comptime arguments, public ABI identity, target-independent fingerprints, incremental invalidation, dedup, and semantic-index facts are explicit and inspectable. Hybrid pass: aliases, imports, AOT, JIT, comptime, cache, and editor tooling project one sema identity relation; there is no codegen-only or LSP-only notion of sameness.
decisions.story: Lena publishes a graph package whose generic module bundles Node, Edge, builders, and algorithms for one weight type. Her app instantiates Graph<String> in two files under different local module names. A Node made by the parser must be accepted by the renderer, incremental builds must reuse one specialization, and rename-only edits must not invalidate caches or make the LSP report a false type mismatch. A security library also needs Graph<String> and Graph<Int> to remain unambiguously different types.

options.name: Applicative instances
options.detail: The same DefinitionId plus the same normalized arguments is one module instance everywhere. ParseGraph.Node and RenderGraph.Node are the same nominal type; both aliases project one InstanceFingerprint, one sema check, one TIR/codegen specialization, one cache entry, and joined LSP references. Different arguments or resolved template definitions remain distinct. Recommended: repeated source spelling means one semantic operation, makes imports/aliases harmless, and gives deterministic dedup without weakening nominal types.

options.name: Generative alias instances
options.detail: Each `module Alias = Template<args>` declaration creates a fresh module identity, even when template and arguments match. Uses and re-exports of that alias share its types, but a second alias declaration receives a distinct InstanceFingerprint and nominal members. Code bodies may deduplicate behind the semantic boundary, while types and LSP references stay separate. This supports deliberate abstraction seals, but ordinary aliases unexpectedly create incompatible values and alias duplication becomes semantic.

options.name: Package-sealed applicative instances
options.detail: The same template application shares within one consuming package, but each downstream package gets a distinct nominal module instance even when DefinitionId and arguments match. All structs, enums, tags, and traits remain nominal. Executable/template-body caches may deduplicate by ApplicationFingerprint across package seals without making types equal. This gives packages an abstraction boundary without making every local alias fresh, but values from two packages cannot cross directly and a re-exported public type carries the consumer package seal.

comparisons.note: OCaml distinguishes applicative paths from generative functor applications; stable paths can share abstract types while fresh applications can create new ones. Jet must choose one default because its ratified syntax has no explicit fresh-application marker.
comparisons.code:
