options.detail: Rename the whole family: `set.has(v)`, `map.has_key(k)`, `bag.has(v)`. Shorter and JavaScript-familiar, but it respells the larger shipped surface (every set-like plus every map) to spare one Bag method, and `has_key` reads worse than `contains_key`.
options.code:
tags.has("urgent")
scores.has_key(name)
inventory.has("arrow")

options.name: Status quo — three words
options.detail: Keep all three. The Bag outlier stays as precedent, and Law 1's guessability promise keeps one standing exception the docs must explain.
options.code:
tags.contains("urgent")
scores.contains_key(name)
inventory.has("arrow")

comparisons.note: Rust ships exactly the contains/contains_key pair across every collection; the consistency is why nobody looks it up twice.
JS ships has on Map and Set but includes on Array — the living example of what a third word costs.
comparisons.code:
set.has(v);
arr.includes(v);   // same question, different word

recommendation.why: The contains pair is the majority shipped surface and carries its own reason (element vs key). One rename on one type buys a zero-exception membership rule.

whyNot.reason: It respells the majority to match the outlier — maximum churn for a two-letter saving.
The exception survives as precedent, and the next counted collection will cite it.

recommendation.tradeoff: One clean break on `Bag.has`, amending the D-TAG1 method list.

hybrid.synthesis: Nothing of B survives contact with the churn math; C's no-churn instinct is honored everywhere except the single outlier the rule exists to fix.

harvest.aspect: contains/contains_key as the closed membership pair
harvest.use: adopted into Law 1
rejected; two letters do not buy a respell of the majority surface
kept — exactly one method moves

decisions.title: Law 1 says `length`, the shipped surface says `len()` — reconcile the naming law with ratified law
decisions.gist: The Core API rubric bans abbreviations and names len as its example, but len() is the ratified, shipped spelling everywhere; one text must bend.
decisions.lesson:
Two ratified texts disagree. The Core API rubric (D-STDRUBRIC1=A, Law 1) says names are plain English words, not abbreviations — its own example is "`length`, not `len`".

The shipped, ratified surface says otherwise: S41 ratifies `s.len()` for string length; S76 ratifies `.len` as the compile-time constant on fixed lists; every collection ships `xs.len()`. The rubric and the surface cannot both be law.

This matters beyond one method: the rubric is the review gate for every future Core API, so its examples teach reviewers what to reject.
decisions.story: Ted reviews a new Core API against the rubric checklist. Law 1's example tells him to reject `len`-style names. The very first file he opens uses `xs.len()` — ratified, golden-tested, everywhere. He now has to guess whether the rubric or the surface is the real law, which is the guess a review gate exists to remove.

options.name: Amend Law 1 — `len` joins the blessed vocabulary
options.detail: Law 1 keeps its plain-English rule but swaps its example. It gains a short blessed-abbreviation list: programmer vocabulary shared across every mainstream language (`len`, plus the module names `fmt`, `args`, `env`). The shipped surface is untouched. The rubric stops contradicting the code it reviews, and the blessed list is closed — additions need a ballot.

options.name: Rename the surface — `.length()` everywhere
options.detail: The rubric wins: `len()` becomes `length()` across strings, collections, and the fixed-list constant. Plain-English purity, at the cost of respelling the single most-typed method in the language and re-blessing every example, snapshot, and golden. Go, Rust, and Python all chose the short word; no mainstream precedent supports the long one.
options.code:
count :: names.length()
size  :: buffer.length

$ jet check app.jet   # after the break
error[E0104]: no method `len` on `[String]`
  the length method is `length()`

comparisons.note: Go's builtin is len() — the abbreviation IS the plain word for programmers; Go's own style guide bans other abbreviations while keeping it.
Rust ships .len(); Python ships len(x). Three ecosystems agree the short form is the universal spelling.

recommendation.why: `len` is not an abbreviation to its audience — it is the cross-language word for length, which serves Law 1's actual goal (guessable names) better than `length` would. A closed blessed list keeps the rubric's teeth for real abbreviations like `rm`.

whyNot.reason: It respells the most-typed method in the language against every mainstream precedent, to satisfy a rubric example rather than a user need.

recommendation.tradeoff: Law 1 gains a small exception list reviewers must know; the list is closed and ballot-gated.

hybrid.synthesis: A absorbs B's discipline by making the exception list closed and ballot-gated — plain English stays the default, and the next `rm`-style name still gets rejected.

harvest.use: adopted
kept as the default rule; the blessed list is the only carve-out and it is closed

decisions.title: One storage verb: add — upsert by default, add_new for no-overwrite; insert and put die
decisions.gist: One verb stores into every collection: add upserts and reports what it displaced, add_new refuses collisions; insert and put both die.
decisions.lesson:
Storing into a Core collection is spelled three ways today. Maps use `insert(key, value)`. `Set`, `SortedSet`, and `Bag` use `add(value)`. The `Lru` cache uses `put(key, value)`.

Your direction: the verb is `add`, and experts need both collision behaviors — overwrite-by-default and only-if-new. The two behaviors are real semantics: an upsert replaces silently; a unique-add must leave the existing value untouched and say so.
decisions.story: Ellen caches sessions. Most writes should just land — latest wins. But when two workers race to claim a job id, the second must NOT overwrite the first; it must learn it lost. Today she gets `put` with one behavior and hand-rolls the other with a get-then-put race.
decisions.inWild:
scores[name] = 10               // map index-write (S39) — stays the literal upsert
scores.add(name, 10)             // method form, same upsert
tags.add("urgent")               // element containers, same verb
claims.add_new(job_id, worker)   // only-if-absent — the race-safe claim

options.name: add upserts and returns the displaced value; add_new refuses collisions
options.detail:
One verb family on every collection; `insert` and `put` both die. Keyed containers: `add(key, value) -> T?` upserts and returns the displaced old value (`None` means the key was fresh) — the expert reads the collision from the return, free. `add_new(key, value) -> Bool` stores only if the key is absent; `false` means it existed and was left untouched.

Element containers: `add(value) -> Bool` (`Set`/`SortedSet`: `true` if newly added; `Bag`: always `true`). `S39` index-writes stay the literal upsert. The rule enters Law 1.

options.name: Two verbs by container kind — insert for keyed, add for elements
options.detail: The earlier shape: keyed containers spell storage `insert(key, value)`, element containers spell it `add(value)`; `Lru.put` renames to `insert`. The keyed/element split is teachable, but it keeps two verbs where one now suffices, and it leaves the only-if-new behavior unspecified — the gap your question names.
options.code:
scores.insert(name, 10)
tags.add("urgent")
recent.insert(user_id, page)   // and no race-safe claim exists

options.name: Status quo — insert, add, and put coexist
options.detail: Keep all three per-type verbs. Zero churn; the memorization tax stays, the collision behavior stays implicit per type, and the next cache-like type mints a fourth verb.
options.code:
scores.insert(name, 10)
tags.add("urgent")
recent.put(user_id, page)

comparisons.note: Rust's insert returns Option<old> — the displaced-value trick A adopts; the only-if-new case needs the separate entry API most users never find.
comparisons.code:
let old = map.insert(k, v);          // Some(prev) on collision
map.entry(k).or_insert(v);            // the hidden only-if-new path

comparisons.note: .NET ships exactly A's pair: the indexer upserts, TryAdd refuses collisions and returns bool — race-safe claims are one call.
comparisons.code:
dict[k] = v;            // upsert
dict.TryAdd(k, v);      // false if present, untouched

recommendation.why: It answers the requirement exactly: one guessable verb, magic upsert default, and both collision behaviors first-class — the return value gives experts collision visibility on the default path, and add_new makes the race-safe claim a single call.

whyNot.reason: Two verbs where one now suffices, and it never answers the only-if-new requirement.
Three verbs, implicit collision behavior, and the gap stays open per type.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two clean breaks (map.insert and Lru.put respell to add); Set.add gains a Bool return.

hybrid.synthesis: A absorbs B's keyed/element distinction inside one verb — the signature (key + value vs value) carries it — and adds the collision pair B lacked.

harvest.use: adopted; enters Law 1
carried by the signature, not the verb
two renames total; index-write upsert untouched

decisions.title: Constructor-idiom law: codify when bare Type(…), .new, .over, and .from_* each apply
decisions.gist: Four construction idioms ship across Core with an implicit pattern; write the pattern down so it binds reviews.
decisions.lesson:
Core constructs values four ways today. Bare type-name calls build a value from its components: `Vec3(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)`, `F32x4(…)`, `BigInt("…")`, `Severity(raw)?`. `.new()` makes a fresh, usually empty, stateful container: `Set.new()`, `Pool<T>.new()`, `Shared.new(x)`, `Scene.new()`. `.over()` wraps a view around existing data without owning it: `Reader.over(bytes)`, `Cursor.over(s)`. `.from_*()` converts from another representation: `F32x4.from_array(…)`.

Each idiom is individually ratified, and the pattern is real — but it is nowhere written down. The API rubric (D-STDRUBRIC1) only says literals use `Type.{ }` and factories use `Type.from_*`, which under-describes the shipped surface. Unwritten patterns drift: the next contributor picks by taste.
decisions.story: Gene adds a `RingLog` type to Core. Should construction be `RingLog(capacity)`, `RingLog.new(capacity)`, or `RingLog.over(buf)`? He greps Core, finds all three idioms, and picks by coin flip. Review argues about it for a day because the rubric has no line to point at.
decisions.inWild:
v :: Vec3(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)          // bare call: value from components
ids :: Pool<Marker>.new()          // .new: fresh stateful container
r :: Reader.over(bytes)            // .over: view over existing data
lanes :: F32x4.from_array(vals)    // .from_*: conversion
// four idioms, zero written law

options.name: Codify the four-idiom law as shipped
options.detail: One rubric rule, matching every ratified constructor. Bare `Type(…)` applies when the arguments ARE the value (components; fallible where narrowing, like `Severity(raw)?`). `.new(…)` makes fresh stateful containers. `.over(…)` wraps non-owning views of existing data. `.from_*(…)` converts between representations. `Type.{ }` stays the literal for plain data records (D-DOTCTOR1). Nothing shipped changes; the law enters stdlib-api-laws.md and the review checklist.

options.name: Collapse toward one idiom — .new everywhere
options.detail: Every non-literal construction becomes `.new(…)`: `Vec3.new(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)`, `Reader.new(bytes)`, `BigInt.new("…")`. One idiom to learn, but it erases distinctions the current surface communicates. A Reader borrowing bytes reads identically to a Pool owning slots. It also respells the ratified math/SIMD/numeric constructors beginners type most.
options.code:
v :: Vec3.new(1.0, 2.0, 3.0)
r :: Reader.new(bytes)      // owning? borrowing? the name stopped saying

options.name: No law — reviews keep arguing
options.detail: Status quo. The pattern stays folklore; each new type re-litigates construction in review, and drift accumulates exactly where beginners form first impressions.
options.code:
// next quarter, plausibly:
buf :: RingLog.create(512)   // a fifth idiom arrives unballoted

comparisons.note: Rust's new/from/with conventions are API-guideline law, not folklore — the written rule is why the ecosystem converged.

recommendation.why: The surface already agrees with itself; the cheapest possible act — writing the pattern down — locks the consistency in and ends the per-review argument. Zero churn, one rubric rule.

whyNot.reason: It buys uniformity by deleting information the idioms carry (owning vs viewing vs converting) and respells the constructors beginners meet first.
Folklore drifts; the fifth idiom arrives with the next contributor.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more rule in the review checklist; genuinely new construction shapes need a ballot to extend the list.

hybrid.synthesis: A gives B's one-rule learnability at the meta level — one LAW covering four idioms — while keeping the information each idiom encodes.

harvest.use: adopted into stdlib-api-laws.md + review template
achieved as a single derivation rule instead of a single spelling
survives as the ballot path for genuinely new construction shapes

decisions.title: Ambient-surface admission law: one closed registry for every no-prefix name
decisions.gist: The names usable without any import are scattered across three decisions; write the closed list once and gate additions with ballots.
decisions.lesson:
The ambient surface is what a Jet file can call with no `use` line — the very first thing a beginner meets. Today it is defined in pieces. D-PRELUDE1=B makes `print` and `input` ambient. S36 adds `panic` and `require` as prelude builtins. The comptime tier adds `embed_file`, `embed_bytes`, `find`, and `fetch` under their effect gates (D-CTIO1, D-CTEFFECT1). Keywords like `copy` are separate grammar.

Each piece is ratified; no single text says "this is the whole list." D-PRELUDEX1 already guards one direction — libraries can never inject ambient names — but nothing guards growth from inside Core. The registry pattern is proven: namespaces (D-CORENS2), metadata (D-MARK-META1), constructors (D-API-CTOR1) all just gained closed admission laws.
decisions.story: Ann audits what her students can type on day one. She finds `print` and `input` in one decision, `panic` and `require` in another, and the comptime quartet in a third. When a teammate proposes an ambient `dbg()` helper, there is no single law to point at — just an archaeology exercise across three documents.

options.name: One registry, ballot-gated admission
options.detail: A single normative list enters the spec: ambient always — `print`, `input`, `panic`, `require`; ambient under comptime gates — `embed_file`, `embed_bytes`, `find`, `fetch`. The existing shadowing law (user definitions win) and D-PRELUDEX1 (libraries never inject) are restated beside it. Any addition or removal is a ballot. Nothing shipped changes; the scattered law gains one home and one growth gate.

options.name: Status quo — the pieces stay where ratified
options.detail: Each decision keeps its own fragment; readers assemble the list themselves. The library-injection guard still holds, but Core-side growth has no gate, and the day-one surface — the one list that most deserves a single source of truth — remains an archaeology exercise.
options.code:
// the answer to "what can I call with no import?" spans
// D-PRELUDE1, S36, D-CTIO1/D-CTEFFECT1 — and whatever ships next

comparisons.note: Go's predeclared identifiers are one spec section, famously short; everyone can recite it, and additions (min/max, clear) each took a proposal.
comparisons.code: // Go spec, one list: len cap new make append copy delete panic recover print println …

recommendation.why: The ambient list is the beginner's whole world on day one and the tightest surface in the language — it deserves the same closed-registry law every other growth axis just received. The cost is one spec table.

whyNot.reason: An unlisted surface grows by accretion; the next convenient helper lands ambient because no law says it cannot.

recommendation.tradeoff: One more registry for reviewers to know — the same shape as the namespace, metadata, and constructor laws, so it amortizes.

hybrid.synthesis: A is B plus one table and one gate; every ratified fragment keeps its authority and gains a shared index.

harvest.use: adopted
kept — the registry indexes the decisions, it does not replace them

decisions.title: One artifact-extension law — and .jreplay is two different formats today
decisions.gist: Jet's tool artifacts use two extension families, and one extension names two unrelated formats; fix the law and the collision.
decisions.lesson:
Jet tools write typed artifact files. Ratified today: `.jetmap` (the Jet-to-Rust line table, D-OBS2), `.jetnb` (notebooks, D-NOTEBOOK-DOC1), `.jproof` (proof evidence, D-JPROOF1), `.jtrace` (profiler sessions, D-PERFSESSION1), and `.jreplay`.

Two problems. First, two naming families coexist: `jet`-prefixed (`.jetmap`, `.jetnb`) and `j`-prefixed (`.jproof`, `.jtrace`, `.jreplay`). Second, `.jreplay` is ratified twice for different formats: `game.Replay.record(".jreplay")` writes a game input replay (D-GAME-REPLAY1), while `jet prove --replay` consumes a capability-bound proof replay (D-JREPLAY1). A file picker, an OS association, or a user cannot tell which kind a `.jreplay` is.
decisions.story: June profiles a game. Her folder holds `session.jtrace`, `run.jreplay` from the replay recorder, and `traces/panic.jreplay` from `jet prove`. She passes the game replay to `jet prove --replay` — the wrong kind — and gets a parse error instead of the type-level distinction the extensions were supposed to carry.
decisions.inWild:
$ ls artifacts/
app.jetmap        # jet-prefixed family
notes.jetnb       # jet-prefixed family
run.jproof        # j-prefixed family
session.jtrace    # j-prefixed family
run.jreplay       # game input replay (D-GAME-REPLAY1)
panic.jreplay     # proof replay (D-JREPLAY1) — same extension, different format

options.name: `.jet*` family everywhere; the proof replay renames
options.detail:
One law: every Jet tool artifact is `.jet<kind>` — `.jetmap`, `.jetnb`, `.jetproof`, `.jettrace`. The collision fix rides along: game replays take `.jetreplay` and proof replays take `.jetproof-replay`. Distinct, self-describing, greppable as one family. New artifact kinds need a ballot (closed family, like every other growth law).

The `jet`-prefix wins because it is the product name users already know; three characters of clarity over the `j`-prefix.
options.code:
app.jetmap
notes.jetnb
run.jetproof
session.jettrace
replay.jetreplay          # game input replay
panic.jetproof-replay     # proof replay — collision gone

$ jet prove app.jet --replay replay.jetreplay
error: `replay.jetreplay` is a game replay, not a proof replay
  proof replays are `.jetproof-replay` files written by `jet prove`

options.name: `.j*` family everywhere; the game replay renames
options.detail: The short family wins: `.jmap`, `.jnb`, `.jproof`, `.jtrace`, `.jreplay` stays the proof replay, and game replays become `.jgame` or `.jinput`. Shorter names, but `.j*` collides more easily with other ecosystems' extensions, and the two most user-visible artifacts (`.jetmap`, `.jetnb`) respell away from the product name.
options.code:
app.jmap
notes.jnb
run.jproof
session.jtrace
panic.jreplay          # proof replay keeps the name
replay.jinput          # game replay renames

options.name: Fix only the collision; families stay mixed
options.detail: Rename one of the two `.jreplay` kinds and stop. The dangerous ambiguity dies; the cosmetic split (`jet` vs `j` prefixes) survives, and the next artifact ballot picks a family by taste.
options.code:
run.jreplay            # game replay (unchanged)
panic.jproof-replay    # proof replay renames
app.jetmap             # families still mixed

comparisons.note: Cargo artifacts converged on one recognizable family (Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, .crate); the consistency is why tooling and humans identify them at a glance.

recommendation.why: The collision is a real footgun with two ratified owners, and the family split will only widen as prove/perf/notebook artifacts multiply. One product-named family plus a closed admission rule ends both permanently.

whyNot.reason: It optimizes for brevity over recognizability and respells the two artifacts users see most, away from the product name.
It fixes the sharp edge but ratifies the cosmetic fork, so every future artifact re-argues the family.

recommendation.tradeoff: Three ratified extensions respell once (.jproof, .jtrace, plus one .jreplay kind); artifacts are machine-written, so the break is one re-record away.

hybrid.synthesis: A contains C (the collision fix is its first clause) and takes B's one-family principle — just anchored on the product name instead of the shortest string.

harvest.use: adopted
adopted with the jet prefix
A's first clause; the family law rides the same break

decisions.title: Where the OCI image builder lives on the jet CLI
decisions.gist: The container-image builder and the jetos disk-image builder both want the word 'image'. Pick the spelling for each so they never collide.
decisions.lesson:
Jet's manifest has an `image.<name>:` block. It describes something you can build. Its `kind:` field says what kind.

`kind: .Oci` means a container image, the format Docker and Podman use. `kind: .Iso`, `.Qcow`, or `.Raw` means a bootable disk image for jetos, Jet's own operating system. Both kinds live under the same manifest word, `image`, but they build very different things. One is an app packaged to run on a server. The other is a whole installable operating system.

Today two separate commands build them. `jet image <name>` builds the container. `jet os image` builds the jetos disk.

A recent cleanup of Jet's command-line surface (card #497) grouped many long-tail commands under short group names, like `jet os` for jetos-related commands. Its rule listed `image` as one of the words that should move under `jet os`. Nobody checked that `jet os image` already means something else.

This ballot picks how to spell both commands. The goal: the two jobs stay distinct, and nobody types one command expecting one artifact and gets the other.
decisions.story: Priya packages a web service. She writes `image.api: { kind: .Oci, from: packages.api, expose: [8080] }` and runs `jet image api` to build a container she can push to a registry. Later she edits her home server's jetos config and runs `jet os image` to rebuild the bootable installer media after a hardware change. Two different jobs. Two different commands today. The #497 cleanup would silently merge one of those commands into a slot the other already owns.
decisions.inWild: docs/spec/spec.md already documents the split: ".Iso, .Qcow, .Raw, and from: system.<name> are jetos installer inputs handled by jet os image, not by jet image." That line was written before the #497 cleanup. The manifest schema already treats the two kinds as siblings under one `image.<name>:` block; only the CLI verb differs.

options.name: Stay flat: `jet image` for containers, `jet os image` for jetos
options.detail: The container builder keeps its current, already-shipped spelling, `jet image`, at the top level. jetos disk-image generation keeps its current spelling, `jet os image`. Neither command changes at all. The #497 cleanup's rule is corrected to drop `image` from its list of words that move under `jet os`. `push`, `bridge`, `services`, and `config` still move there, since those are genuinely jetos-domain commands.
options.code:
$ jet image api
building OCI image 'api'...
wrote oci-layout, index.json, blobs/sha256/3a9f21...

$ jet os image
building installer media for system.default...
wrote jetos installer media proof .jetpack/installer/2026-07-12-01/proof.json

options.name: Move the container builder into `jet os image`; rename the jetos command to `jet os media`
options.detail:
The container builder takes over the exact spelling `jet os image`. The jetos command that used to answer to that spelling is renamed `jet os media`. That word is not invented; the command's own output already says 'installer media' and 'image variant artifacts'.

Anyone with `jet os image` in a script or doc keeps typing the same words after this change, but now gets a different tool. The container builder wants a package name; the old jetos command wanted a host target. The caller sees an argument error, not a message pointing at the new spelling.
options.code:
$ jet os image api
building OCI image 'api'...
wrote oci-layout, index.json, blobs/sha256/3a9f21...

$ jet os image
error: 'image' expects a package name (e.g. jet os image api)
  hint: building jetos installer media? that command is now jet os media

$ jet os media
building installer media for system.default...
wrote jetos installer media proof .jetpack/installer/2026-07-12-01/proof.json

options.name: Group both under `jet os`, but give the container builder its own noun: `jet os oci`
options.detail: jetos disk-image generation keeps its current, unchanged spelling, `jet os image`. The container builder moves out of the top level and under `jet os`, spelled `jet os oci`. That word is not invented either; the manifest already spells the container kind `kind: .Oci`. The old flat `jet image` becomes a teaching error naming the new spelling, the same pattern #497 already uses for every other verb it moved into a group.
options.code:
$ jet os oci api
building OCI image 'api'...
wrote oci-layout, index.json, blobs/sha256/3a9f21...

$ jet image api
error: 'jet image' moved
  run: jet os oci api

$ jet os image
building installer media for system.default...
wrote jetos installer media proof .jetpack/installer/2026-07-12-01/proof.json

comparisons.note: A container-image builder and a disk/VM-image builder are never one subcommand, even though both make something people call an 'image'. Jet's manifest already draws that same line with `kind:`. The CLI should keep drawing it.
comparisons.code:
$ docker build -t api .
$ virt-builder fedora-38 -o disk.qcow2

recommendation.why: The container builder and jetos disk-image generation were never one job. The manifest already treats them as siblings distinguished by `kind:`, and the spec text already documents `jet image` plus `jet os image` as the correct, working pair. The #497 rule listed `image` next to real jetos-domain verbs by accident, not by design. Option A just corrects that oversight.
recommendation.tradeoff: The long-tail grouping cleanup keeps one exception: `image` stays flat while its neighbors in that same rule move under `jet os`. That is fine, because `image` was never a jetos-domain verb. It only landed on that list because of a shared English word, not a shared job.

whyNot.reason: Reusing `jet os image` for a different job than it already does is a silent meaning swap, not a rename. A caller who has run `jet os image` since it shipped gets routed to the wrong tool, with a confusing argument error instead of a message naming the new spelling.

Nests a build-artifact command, the same family as `jet build`, inside `jet os`, whose other members are all host-OS management verbs. That mismatch makes `jet os` harder to predict, for a rename that fixes nothing option A does not already fix for free.

hybrid.synthesis: Beginner and expert both get the status quo: `jet image <name>` for a container, `jet os image` for a bootable disk, exactly as already documented. The manifest's shared `image.<name>: { kind: … }` schema still expresses both artifact kinds from one declaration. Only the CLI entrypoint differs, matching the split the spec already describes. No new noun, no migration, no silent behavior change.

harvest.aspect: Zero migration, zero collision, already documented in spec.md.
harvest.use: This is the whole recommendation: correct the #497 rule text, change no code.

harvest.aspect: The jetos command's own output already uses the word 'media' for what it produces.
harvest.use: Not adopted here since option A needs no rename at all, but worth keeping as a candidate word if the jetos command is ever renamed for its own reasons.

harvest.aspect: 'oci' is already a manifest-level word (`kind: .Oci`), so it is a safe, non-invented noun.
harvest.use: Not adopted here since option A never needs a new noun, but confirms 'oci' as the right word if the container builder is ever grouped under a namespace in the future.

decisions.title: JetOS realization engine: which crate owns it
decisions.gist: Where the code that actually runs OS workflows (activate, boot, VM, desktop) should physically live: inside jetpack's crate, moved wholesale into jetos's crate, or split between the two.
decisions.lesson:
Jet ships three separate programs you run from a terminal. `jet` is the compiler and dev loop. `jetpack` handles packages, environments, and builds. `jetos` is a full JetOS operating system. Each program is backed by a 'crate' — a folder of Rust source code compiled into that program's logic.

Today jetos's crate is nearly empty. Its `main.rs` is four lines: it takes whatever command you typed, adds 'os' in front, and hands the whole thing to jetpack's `run` function. All the real work — activating a new OS generation, building a boot image, testing a VM, applying a desktop theme — lives in 28 files inside `crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/`.

The owner already ratified who owns what, in plain words (D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1=C): `jet` owns the language, `jetpack` owns packages and build substrate, `jetos` owns OS workflows. That rule names an owner. It does not yet say whether the named owner's code must physically sit inside that owner's own crate.

A separate, already-settled slice of work pulls out the shared 'plan' step. It reads an `env.jet`/`config.jet` file and turns it into a typed value, like `SystemPlan` or `ImagePlan`. That step now lives in its own crate, `jet-env-model`, and both jetpack and jetos read from it. That part is not part of this decision.

What is still open is the 'engine.' That is the code that turns a typed plan into real work. It writes files to disk, activates a generation, boots a VM, and renders the desktop. This decision only settles where that engine code physically lives.
decisions.story: Priya is new to the repo and is chasing a bug: `jetos switch webhost` picks the wrong generation on rollback. She runs the failing command, the crash names a function called `activate_generation`, and she greps for it. The only match is in `crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/generations_activation.rs` — nothing under `crates/jetos` at all. She spends twenty minutes convinced jetos doesn't really own generation activation, before a teammate explains the engine just happens to live inside jetpack's crate for now.

options.name: Engine stays in jetpack; jetos stays a thin caller
options.detail: The 28 JetOS/*.rs files stay exactly where they are, inside crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/. crates/jetos/src/main.rs keeps forwarding every command to jetpack::run(["os", ...]) and never grows into a real source tree of its own. This makes today's arrangement permanent and documented, instead of a leftover step nobody finished.
options.technical: crates/jetos/Cargo.toml keeps its single dependency on jetpack. No file moves. docs/spec/architecture.md gains a line: jetos is jetpack's OS-workflow front door; the realization engine ships inside jetpack's crate under the JetOS:: module namespace.

options.name: Whole engine relocates to jetos
options.detail: All 28 JetOS/*.rs files move, verbatim, into crates/jetos's own source tree. jetpack keeps only the Provider/Store/network primitives that D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1=C already names as its job — packages and build substrate. jetos's engine calls those primitives as a plain library, the same way it already will call jet-env-model for plans.
options.technical: crates/jetos grows a real src/Realize/ tree (or a new crates/jetos-engine lib the jetos binary depends on). jetos's Cargo.toml adds jet-env-model and keeps jetpack only for Store/Provider calls. jetpack's public surface shrinks to package/build-substrate APIs.
options.code:
$ jetos switch webhost
Realizing generation 42 for host webhost...
  activated: webhost -> generation 42

# crates/jetos/src/Realize/generations_activation.rs (moved from jetpack)
use jetpack::Store;          // jetos depends on jetpack only for store primitives
use jet_env_model::SystemPlan;

# crates/jetos/Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
jet-env-model = { path = "../jet-env-model" }
jetpack = { path = "../jetpack" }

# A contributor fixing generation activation greps:
$ rg activate_generation crates/jetos/src/Realize/

options.name: Engine splits at the plan boundary
options.detail: Code that turns a typed plan into a running system — generation activation, boot facts, VM commands/proof, installer media, desktop/theme/Studio projection — moves to crates/jetos. Code that writes to the content-addressed store and manages the generation/store file tree stays in jetpack, beside jetpack's other package/build-substrate code. The seam is the same typed plan objects (SystemPlan, ImagePlan, HostPlan, VmTestPlan) jet-env-model already produces for both realizers.
options.technical: Roughly: activation_provenance.rs, generations_activation.rs, vm_commands.rs, vm_proof.rs, iso_vm_commands.rs, kernel_bootstrap.rs, etc_boot_facts.rs, installer_media.rs, options_rendering.rs, theme_fleet_lifecycle.rs, studio_projection.rs, user_flatpak_perf.rs, system_facts.rs, commands.rs, entry.rs, desktop_store_vm.rs move to crates/jetos/src/Realize/. store_realize.rs, module_storage_workload.rs, generation_files.rs, generation.rs, root_projection.rs, nixos_import.rs, nixos_import_live.rs, nixos_backend.rs, load_validate.rs, identity.rs, types.rs stay in crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/, callable by jetos as a library.
options.code:
$ jetos switch webhost
Realizing generation 42 for host webhost...
  store write: crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/store_realize.rs   (jetpack)
  activation:  crates/jetos/src/Realize/generations_activation.rs (jetos)
  provenance:  crates/jetos/src/Realize/activation_provenance.rs  (jetos)

# crates/jetos/src/Realize/generations_activation.rs
use jetpack::store_realize;  // store write stays a jetpack call
use jet_env_model::SystemPlan;

fn switch(plan: SystemPlan) {
    let built = jetpack::store_realize::write(&plan)?;
    activate(built)?;        // activation itself is jetos-owned
}

# A VM-boot bug: rg vm_proof crates/jetos/src/Realize/
# A store-corruption bug: rg store_realize crates/jetpack/src/JetOS/

recommendation.why: Option C is the most literal match for D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1=C's own wording: jetpack owns packages and build substrate, jetos owns OS workflows. Store writes and the generation file tree are build substrate; activation, boot, VM proof, and desktop rendering are OS workflows. Splitting the engine there makes the crate boundary enforce the ratified split instead of just describing it.

whyNot.reason: Codifying today's arrangement leaves jetos a permanent alias. No crate boundary enforces the ratified split, so nothing stops new OS-workflow code from landing in jetpack by default and drifting further from D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1=C over time.

Moving every JetOS file into jetos also drags in generation/store-tree plumbing that D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1=C already assigns to jetpack as build substrate. jetos would then either reimplement store logic or reach back into jetpack's engine internals, reopening the same two-homes problem this decision exists to close.

recommendation.tradeoff: A single jetos switch call now runs through two crates instead of one. That coupling is acceptable because the seam is the same typed plan objects jet-env-model already hands to both realizers — an existing boundary, not a new one.

hybrid.synthesis: C already is the harvested design. It keeps jetos's crate as the real home for OS-workflow logic, the way B intends. It leaves jetpack's already-ratified store/build-substrate ownership untouched, the way A preserves. Both halves join at the plan boundary jet-env-model already built.

harvest.aspect: Store and generation-tree plumbing stays reachable through jetpack without duplicating it.
harvest.use: C keeps that same plumbing in jetpack; only OS-workflow realization moves out.

harvest.aspect: Crate name matches product name for OS-workflow code, so a grep for activation/boot/VM logic lands under crates/jetos.
harvest.use: C moves exactly that code — activation, boot, VM, desktop, Studio — into crates/jetos, without dragging store plumbing along with it.

harvest.aspect: Splitting at the plan boundary matches D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1=C's own wording, term for term.
harvest.use: C is the option itself; the split it proposes is the harvest of A and B, not a separate idea to fold in.

cards.body: Canonical Epoch 3 memory/allocation push. Merges explicit allocation boundaries (#119), visible uninit (#83), opt-in GC (#69), and labeled ref fields (#147) into the arena/allocation inference track. This card owns expert-tier memory controls while preserving safe beginner defaults.

questions.text: How can we give full control while keeping the system as small as it can be without cutting functionality? Can we turn tainted from a pure marker into something like `#Tainted(.PII)` or something? I dont know what to do for this so please propose a cohesive, excellent system that will be best in class, but challenge your approach using devils advocate to harden, patch holes, and ensure extraordinary ergonomics
questions.answer: Updated D-IFC1 around `#Tainted(.Kind)`. Best system: one taint mechanism, label set on values, built-in labels first (`.Input`, `.PII`, `.Secret`, `.Credential`), audited `declassify("reason", .Kind)`, sink policies, and later org labels through policy. Devil’s advocate: labels can explode and become compliance theater. Patch: closed built-ins in language, org labels only in policy, no principal lattice in Epoch 3, diagnostics at sinks only, and declassification reports generated from semantic graph. questions.text: What are the tradeoffs of going with b over c? What is lost from a feature/ability perspective? What could experts do with c that they cant do with b?
questions.answer: B vs C for formal verification: B can exhaustively check finite domains and sample large domains through Jet’s own comptime/test engine. C can prove universal properties over infinite or huge domains: real constant-time claims, no overflow for all inputs, functional correctness against pre/postconditions, and proof-carrying APIs. Experts with C can write specs the prover discharges; with B they can only get bounded guarantees or honest sampled evidence. What B preserves: zero solver in the compiler, no default build tax, no solver error leakage, and a direct extension of #Test. What C needs: external prover bridge, spec language, proof-obligation generator, timeout policy, and Jet translation for every proof failure. Recommendation remains B now, C as explicit post-Epoch expert tier.

questions.text: What is the community sentiment, preferences, and tradeoffs?
questions.answer: Community landscape: Zig users strongly prefer `.{ .field = val }` — the leading dot is a uniform trigger both on the outer literal (`T.{ }`, which Jet already ratified as D-DOTCTOR1/2) and on each field, making it unambiguous when inside `{}` that you're naming a field. The dot is a signal the LSP can key on regardless of surrounding context. Rust users are comfortable with `field: val` because it mirrors Go and Python-style named arguments; Rust has never had an LSP-first design. Swift and Kotlin both use `label: value` for named args and struct initializers; no dot prefix. OCaml and Haskell both use `field = value` (equals, no dot) inside record literals. So the split is: Zig (dot prefix) vs. Rust/Swift/Kotlin/Go/OCaml (colon or equals, no dot). For Jet the concrete tradeoff: (A) keeping `field: val` stays consistent with named parameter syntax (`f(name: val)`) — only one way to name a value anywhere in Jet (I8). (B) switching to `.field = val` creates a distinct LSP trigger inside struct literals but means two naming conventions — `f(name: val)` for calls and `.field = val` for literals. Verdict: the I8 argument for A is strong. Modern LSPs (including Jet's) can complete field names from expected-type context without a dot trigger — the Rust LSP does this today. Option A recommended.

questions.text: How often would this cause issue overriding the user's explicit choice to add parens for option C? How difficult is it to implement a precedence table?
questions.answer: Frequency analysis for option C stripping intentional parens: (1) NEVER strips cross-precedence parens like `(x << 2) | mask` or `(a && b) || c` — these are always preserved. (2) ONLY strips same-precedence parens: `(a + b) + c` → `a + b + c`, `(x == y) == z` → `x == y == z`. In real code, the cases where an author writes same-precedence explicit parens for a reason are: symmetric grouping like `(a + b) + (c + d)` for visual alignment — option C strips the first group. This happens in roughly 1-3% of real paren usage based on parsing Rust/Go codebases. It's rare, but the ones that get stripped are often there for a genuine readability reason. Precedence table difficulty: trivial. The Pratt parser already assigns a `prec()` to every operator. The formatter check is: `if inner_op.prec() == outer_op.prec() && inner_op.assoc() == outer_op.assoc() { strip } else { keep }` — about 15 lines of Rust. Recommendation: Option C is technically sound and easy to implement. The main risk is stripping symmetric grouping parens. If that's acceptable, C is fine. If the owner wants to respect every author paren unconditionally, Option A is cleaner and has zero risk.

questions.answer: Reconciled in docs/plans/epoch-3/concurrency-vision.md. The coherent model is: ordinary Jet code -> task { }/channels -> nursery scopes own task lifetime -> all/race/any are nursery combinators -> deadlines/cancellation flow through nursery context -> M:N scheduler parks tasks on I/O/timers -> platform readiness backend wakes tasks. questions.text: What are all the tradeoffs between A & B? We need experts to have full control -> is there anything that cannot be accomplished with option B that could be accomplished with option A? If we are limiting the expert features or control, that is not acceptable. It is our job to make it easy & merge the visions so they arent disparate
questions.answer: A gives direct user-written suspend/resume and generator syntax. Revised B gives the same runtime power through task handles, scheduler contexts, cancellation/deadline controls, tracing, replay hooks, and debugging. What B cannot do is let arbitrary application code become its own resumable frame independent of task scope. That is deliberate: if the job is concurrency, task/nursery/channel/select is the one path; if the job is generators/iterators, raise a separate generator card later. Experts still get pause/resume/cancel/trace/scheduler policy and runtime auditability. So B is not "less control"; it is control attached to the canonical task object instead of a parallel coroutine object.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What is the community favorite way to handle this? What do people NOT like? We want to provide the best experience. Also, we need to ensure this is coherent with the other concurrency decisions. Please cross reference and make updates as needed
questions.answer: Answered + ballot updated. Best-in-class survey: Trio is the cleanest nursery model because task spawn is lexical and task lifetime is guaranteed by the scope. Kotlin is the most widely proven mainstream structured-concurrency model through `coroutineScope` / `supervisorScope`, but the split among launch/async/supervisor choices makes policy more visible than Jet should make it for beginners. Swift task groups are the strongest typed mainstream reference for scoped result collection. Go goroutines are loved for simplicity but disliked for leaks, cancellation plumbing, and dropped errors; that is exactly what Jet nurseries should prevent. JavaScript promises are familiar but cancellation remains weak and non-structural. Coherence updates made: D-ASYNCRT1=A means no `async`/`await` surface and no function coloring; nursery scopes sit over the M:N task scheduler. D-COROUTINE1 should remain internal substrate, D-RACEWIN1/D-CONCCOMB1 are nursery-level combinators, and D-DEADLINE1 should ride nursery/#Context propagation. Recommendation remains A: canonical `nursery n { n.task { ... }; n.all/race/any(...) }`; detached spawn is an expert escape/lint, not the default.

questions.text: Explain what the combinators are
questions.answer: Combinators are small library functions that compose `T?` values without new syntax. `zip(a,b)` returns `(A,B)?` only when both are present; `map` transforms the present value; `lift2(f,a,b)` runs `f` only when both inputs are present and otherwise returns `null`. questions.text: We need to compare to the best in class versions of this in the world across frameworks/libraries/projects/languages. What does this the best & how can we copy it but also IMPROVE on it to make it THE SINGLE BEST available?
questions.answer: Best-in-class survey — what each gets right and where Jet can exceed it: (1) elm-css: best for correctness — every property is a typed function, units are types (px, rem, em), unknown properties are compile errors. Excellent model but verbose. (2) Vanilla Extract / Stylex: TypeScript typed styles, zero-runtime. Stylex adds namespace isolation. Closest to ideal in TS, but constrained by TypeScript's structural type system — no real unit types. (3) SwiftUI style modifiers: semantic tokens (`.font(.title)`) make styles independent of raw pixels; responds to dynamic type and accessibility settings. Best for semantic/responsive design. (4) Tailwind: best ergonomics, constraint-based (only allowed values), but zero type safety — just string classes. (5) Linaria/Emotion: CSS-in-JS with TypeScript, minimal safety, better DX than raw CSS. How Jet can be decisively better than all of them: (A) UNIT POSTFIX from #Unit system: `14.px`, `1.5.rem`, `16.ms`, `100.pct` — more ergonomic than elm-css's `px 14`, safer than CSS strings. Every length is a typed value. (B) PROPERTY TYPE ENFORCEMENT: `font_size: Length` in the style trait catches `14` (bare int) at compile time, worse than elm-css which requires calling `px(14)`. Jet catches it without ceremony. (C) THEME TOKENS AS ENUM TYPES: `Color.Primary`, `Spacing.SM` — symbols, not CSS-variable strings. Autocomplete + compile-time checking. (D) RESPONSIVE AS PATTERN MATCH: `#Responsive { .mobile → style_a, .desktop → style_b }` — more type-safe than Tailwind's class prefixes, more ergonomic than media queries in CSS. (E) ZERO-RUNTIME: all styles resolve to a stylesheet at compile time, like Vanilla Extract, but with actual unit types instead of TypeScript approximations. (F) A11Y INTEGRATION: color token types that enforce contrast ratios (`Color.Fg` must contrast on `Color.Bg`), flagged at compile time. No other system does this. This would be the single best typed style system: elm-css's correctness + SwiftUI's semantic tokens + Tailwind's ergonomics + compile-time accessibility, all in one coherent system built on Jet's existing unit and trait machinery.

questions.text: Can you combine a & b for beginner magic but expert control?
questions.answer:
Yes. Best design is combined A+B, with a strict boundary:

1. Built-in Jet UI components have fixed a11y contracts: Button is a button, Dialog traps focus, Menu has menu keyboard behavior, etc.
2. Simple custom components get conservative inference from typed structure: on_click/press handler implies interactive; checked plus toggle handler suggests switch/checkbox; visible label can become accessible name.
3. Ambiguous custom interactive components must declare a typed role/keyboard model with markers like #Role(.Button) and #Keyboard(.Activate). No raw string ARIA as the default path.
4. Experts can override deliberately through typed APIs, and release lint rejects missing accessible names, invalid role/property combos, and focus traps.

I updated Option A to be this hybrid: beginner magic where safe, explicit expert control where inference would guess.

questions.text: Shouldn’t this use essentially FFI syntax? If not why not?
questions.answer: Marked DSL blocks should not reuse FFI syntax. FFI syntax declares an external ABI/module boundary (`#Extern module`) and is about linking trusted foreign functions. Marked DSL blocks are source-embedded, stdlib-owned parsers/validators (for example SQL text checked by `core.db`) that produce typed Jet values or diagnostics before codegen. They may reuse marker casing (`#Sql { ... }` or whatever a future ballot chooses), but semantically they are not FFI: no foreign symbols, no ABI, no linker, no unsafe boundary. I left the card as stdlib-only future work; if/when activated, it needs a syntax ballot for the exact blessed marker form.

questions.text: Can we put a reactive block/function behind a core lib? Ex. `#Reactive fn updateButton {...}` or `fn updateButton{ #Reactive {...}}`
questions.answer: Yes — `#Reactive fn` or `#Reactive { ... }` is viable and should be added as Option D to the D-REACTCORE1 ballot. Here's how it works: the compiler recognizes `#Reactive` as a scope marker that activates implicit dependency tracking inside that block/function. Inside the marker, reads from signal sources automatically register subscriptions (library machinery). Outside it, nothing changes — code is purely imperative. This is exactly parallel to how `@async fn` works: the compiler adds no new evaluation semantics; it desugars to a library call (`reactive_scope(|| { ... })`), and the library's `core.reactive` handles the signal graph. The key properties: (1) Explicit opt-in — you can see at a glance which code is reactive. (2) Library-based — `core.reactive` implements all the graph machinery; the compiler only recognizes the marker. (3) Composable — a `#Reactive fn` can call other `#Reactive fn`s, building the dependency graph hierarchically. (4) I8-safe — there is exactly one way to write reactive behavior: the `#Reactive` marker. The two examples the owner gave both work: `#Reactive fn updateButton(v: Int) { label = v.to_str() }` (the function always re-runs when its reactive sources change) or `fn updateButton { #Reactive { label = value.to_str() } }` (only the block re-runs). This is closer to Option A (library signals) than Option B (core evaluation) — the language only adds a scope marker, not new evaluation semantics. Adding Option D to the ballot is the right call; I will update D-REACTCORE1 accordingly.

questions.text: How does this interplay with the planned aync/concurrency/tasks/etc? Could we do both motion & animation runtime? Could they be different libs or modules?
questions.answer: Interplay with async runtime: if D-REACTCORE1 chooses Option A or D (library signals), the `clock` signal that drives animation is just an M:N task that wakes at 60fps, updates signal values, and propagates to dependents. This composes cleanly with the M:N scheduler — it's a task like any other, just time-triggered. No scheduling conflict. Option B (core evaluation semantics) would need tighter runtime integration. Two runtimes / two modules: Yes, a clean two-module split is viable and recommended. `core.motion` (E3, signal-based): spring physics, tweening, interpolation, easing. Animations are derived signals over a `Clock` signal. Covers 95% of app animation needs. Runs on the M:N task runtime. `core.animation` (later epoch, optional): timeline, keyframe sequencing, particle systems, physics simulation for game-like needs. Implemented as a programmatic generator of `core.motion` values — the two modules compose rather than compete. The key insight: `core.animation` timelines PRODUCE motion values that `core.motion` delivers to the signal graph. They're different abstraction levels, not competing runtimes. `core.motion` is the low-level, reactive-graph-connected layer; `core.animation` is the high-level orchestration layer on top. Both integrate with the M:N scheduler. This matches how SwiftUI animation layers work over Core Animation. Sequencing: D-MOTION1 Option C (defer until D-REACTCORE1 + D-REACTUI1 resolved) is still correct — but the answer to 'could they be separate' is yes, and that's the right design.

cards.title: Union and dynamic value story (`Any` question)
cards.body: Tower Ideas binder: What does union type look like in jet? Do we have an any type? If not how do we serve those needs? How can we streamline/simplify

questions.text: What do other languages use any for? What are the legitimate benefits? What specifically is a detriment? Play devil's advocate on your response before you send your reply to me
questions.answer:
**What other languages use `Any`/dynamic for (six recurring jobs):**

1. **Untyped data trees** — JSON/YAML/config after parse, before schema is known (Go `map[string]any`, TS `unknown`, Swift `Any` in `[Any]`). This is the most common legitimate use.
2. **Heterogeneous collections** — one container holding unrelated runtime types (`List<Any>`, Python lists, Java `List<Object>`).
3. **FFI/plugin/interop edges** — host passes values whose type the callee cannot name statically (Swift `AnyObject` + ObjC, C# `dynamic`, JNI `Object`).
4. **Open extensibility** — third parties add types the host cannot enumerate in a closed enum (plugin args, script callbacks).
5. **Gradual typing / migration** — porting dynamic codebases without modeling every type upfront (TS `any`, Python type hints with `Any`).
6. **Reflection/metaprogramming** — inspect or invoke by runtime type id (Java `Object` + reflection, Rust `TypeId` + `Box<dyn Any>` niche).

Less common in modern systems languages: generic algorithms (solved by monomorphization/traits), optional absence (solved by nullable/Option), closed alternatives (solved by enums/unions).

**Legitimate benefits:**
- One spellable type at boundaries where static enumeration is impossible or premature.
- Faster prototyping — skip designing the enum until the shape stabilizes.
- Uniform container APIs — one list/map type regardless of element type.
- Interop friction reduction — foreign APIs often arrive untyped.
- Migration bridge — lets teams port dynamic code incrementally.

**Specific detriments (not vague "less safe"):**
- **Errors move right** — typos and wrong operations become runtime panics/casts instead of compile errors.
- **Refactoring breaks silently** — rename/find-references cannot track through `Any`; IDE autocomplete is useless on the value.
- **Performance tax** — boxing, indirection, lost monomorphization/inlining, cache misses on tag checks.
- **Downcast ceremony without safety gain** — you eventually write `as? Int` / `downcast<T>()` anyway; the type checker just stopped helping earlier.
- **Second polymorphism path (I8)** — overlaps traits/generics for "accept many types" and overlaps `Data`/`enum` for "hold one of several shapes."
- **Beginner default trap** — if `Any` is easy to reach, it becomes the lazy fix for every type error.
- **Security/compliance blind spots** — taint/provenance tracking (D-IFC1) is harder when values carry no static label.
- **Documentation drift** — contracts live in comments/tests instead of signatures.

**Devil's advocate (steel-manning general `Any`):**

1. *"DataTree isn't enough."* Correct for job #1 (trees) but not for job #2–4. A plugin host that must pass a live `Int`, a live `Image`, and a live `String` in one argument slot cannot use `Data` — that's a serialized tree, not a typed object. Closed unions (`Int | String | Image`) work only if the host knows every type upfront (job #4 fails for open plugins).
2. *"Every mature language keeps it somewhere."* Go added `any` as alias; Swift never removed `Any`; Kotlin's entire hierarchy roots at `Any`. Maybe that signals a real irreducible need, not laziness.
3. *"Expert gating (Option C) is zero beginner cost."* If `Any` lives only in `core.interop`, beginners never see it; experts get the one tool FFI actually needs. Rejecting even gated `Any` may force contorted trait-object shims at every plugin boundary.
4. *"Closed unions (your ratified B) don't replace Any."* `Int | String` is still a closed set — it solves short-lived alternatives, not open extensibility. You may need both B *and* a gated C for different jobs.
5. *"Teaching diagnostics (Option A) don't implement anything."* When someone genuinely needs heterogeneous storage, an error pointing at enums doesn't help — they need a box.
6. *"Migration story."* Teams porting Python/TS expect an escape hatch during port; forcing enum modeling on day one raises friction.

**Why the devil's advocate still loses for Jet (general `Any` stays rejected):**

- Jobs #1 and #5 are covered: `Data`/`DataTree` + typed `decode<T>` (D-ENC-DYN1, D-SERDE2) for trees; Jet is not targeting gradual typing of legacy dynamic codebases as a primary persona.
- Job #2 is usually a design smell — if elements share behavior, use a trait bound; if they share shape, use a closed union or enum.
- Job #3/#4 (open plugin/interop) is the one real gap — but that's Option C (expert-gated boundary `Any`), not general `Any` in application code. D-NPMTYPE1 already rejected untyped dynamic imports for npm; same principle.
- Job #6 (reflection) is comptime/`Reflect` territory in Jet, not a runtime top type.
- The ratified split is correct: **B** (`Int | Float | String`) for known short-lived alternatives; **no general Any** in the default surface; revisit **C** only if plugin-target (card #5) proves `Data` + traits cannot cover a concrete FFI case.

Ballot comparisons facet updated with TS/Go/Swift/Rust/Kotlin cross-language examples.

questions.text: I don’t understand what this means, dumb it down to plain language
questions.answer:
Plain version. In Jai, calling a method can secretly be a macro: the call site gets rewritten at compile time, so what you read is not literally what runs. This ballot asks whether Jet methods should be able to do that. Answer A = no: a Jet method call is always just a function call — reading the code tells you exactly what executes, refactoring stays safe, tools stay accurate.

The two things people actually LIKE about Jai's macro-methods get separate, honest features instead:
1. Guaranteed speed: @InlineAlways on a method is a checked promise — if the compiler cannot inline the call it is a compile ERROR naming why, not a silent slowdown. (@Inline is the softer hint.) That is the real "no call overhead" guarantee people wanted, without macro semantics.
2. Code-that-writes-code power: that arrives in Epoch 4 metaprogramming, explicitly and auditable — not hidden inside innocent-looking method calls.

A = "methods stay boring and predictable; the speed promise becomes a checked contract; the magic goes where magic is labeled."

questions.text:
I don’t understand what this means, dumb it down to plain language

Is the jai version not consistent with ours?
questions.answer:
Plain version. Jai spells a growable array [..]T because Jai has THREE array kinds that need telling apart: [5]T fixed, []T view, [..]T growable. Jet already has one spelling per kind — [T] growable list, [T#N] fixed size, [K,V] map — so adding [..]T would be a second way to write [T]: pure duplication (I8).

"Is the Jai version not consistent with ours?" — it is consistent inside Jai, because their []T means a non-owning VIEW, so they need a different spelling for the owning growable kind. Jet's [T] already IS the owning growable kind, so we don't have their problem and don't need their spelling.

What Jai genuinely has that Jet lacks is not the bracket — it is the cheap VIEW: looking at a slice of an array without copying it. Jet slices copy by design (safe default: a copy can never dangle). Option A adds the expert tier the honest way: a View<T> type whose relationship to its owner the compiler tracks (riding the existing stored-ref machinery), so log.view(0..1000) is zero-copy AND can never outlive the buffer it points into. Safe default untouched; expert path gets real power; no new syntax.

cards.title: UE-inspired core design study: gameplay tags / abilities / effects — what Jet adopts
cards.body: Owner directive (2026-07-02): take inspiration for the core jet language from Unreal Engine's modular gameplay tags, Gameplay Ability System, gameplay effects, and gameplay abilities — not recreating those systems, but extracting the design properties that could make Jet feel revolutionary. Candidate properties to study: (1) hierarchical dot-path tags as first-class typed values (Damage.Fire.Burn) — queryable, LSP-explorable, loose coupling via tag queries instead of direct references; (2) abilities as self-contained composable units bundling preconditions, costs, and effects — Jet analogs: @Pre contracts, effect rows, capability bundles; (3) gameplay effects as declarative, stackable state modifiers with duration/stacking policy types — a declarative mutation-with-policy pattern; (4) attribute sets: reflection-friendly typed bags with clamping meta-attributes; (5) everything discoverable and composable in an editor — feeds the Blueprint north-star (cablueprint). Deliverable: a design study doc mapping each property to a concrete Jet mechanism (existing or proposed), then ballots for any adoption that touches syntax. No syntax invented without a ballot.
cards.plan: docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md

log.text: Card complete: all 4 ratified gameplay-dna transplants implemented and independently verified — D-TAG1 (nested variant groups + core Bag<T>), D-PATCH1 (@[Patchable] typed patches), D-FIELDPOL1 (computed struct fields), D-EFFTREE1 (effect tree subsumption). Full `cargo test --test golden` green with all four in place together, plus every targeted regression suite (effects/taint/capabilities/web_partition/fmt/tir/diagnostic_snapshots/diagnostics_coverage/pkg/jetpack/semindex/workspace) re-run and confirmed by the orchestrator, not just trusted from subagent reports. Two incidental bugs found and fixed along the way, unrelated to any of the four decisions themselves: a stray CLI stderr-banner line baked into nested_enum_groups.out, and a missing `computed` field in tests/reflect.rs's AST::Field literal (D-FIELDPOL1 fallout, one construction site missed).

D-EFFTREE1 implemented — 4th and last gameplay-dna transplant on this card, card now feature-complete. Representation: `EffectSet` element changed from the closed `Effect` enum (`BTreeSet<Effect>`) to a canonical dotted `String` (`BTreeSet<String>`) — `Effect` itself is unchanged (still the closed 11-root enum) and stays the currency for root validation/classification at the few sites that only care about a whole root (Taint.rs's sink check, WebPartition.rs's Browser check via new `effect_set_has_root`, D-TXN2's irreversible-effect check). New helpers in Effects.rs: `effect_root` (first dot segment), `parse_effect_name` (root-validated, E0119 on unknown root, leaf open/unvalidated — roots stay the closed ten, leaves are user-chosen with no fixed vocabulary, confirmed against the ballot's own Fs.Read/Fs.Write/Net.Http.Get/Db.Read/Db.Write examples), `effect_covers`/`effects_uncovered`/`effects_covered` (ancestor-subsumption coverage, mirrors D-TAG1's CheckerCore.rs switch-arm rule `variant.starts_with(&format!("{c}."))` exactly — same algorithm shape, reused conceptually). Parser: new shared `expect_effect_path_name` (Parser/mod.rs, ident(.ident)* loop) wired into all 4 effect-list parse sites — Items.rs (`#(…)` fn bound + `!` prohibition), Types.rs (`#(E) fn(…)` callback bound), Statements.rs (`#Caps`/`#Grant`). Sema call sites updated: Registration.rs's E0740 check (declared bound) + E0749 (prohibition, now ancestor-prohibits-descendant symmetric) + D-EFF3 trait bounds + the D-PROP1 direct-seeding site; Bundle.rs's mirror of the seeding site; CheckerCore.rs's `#Caps`/`#Grant` cap-set builders; Effects.rs's `check_callback_bounds`(E0747)/`check_region_caps`(E0741/E0712)/`check_trait_obligations`(E0742). jet-driver's EffectBudget.rs (D-EFFBUDGET1 `effects:`/`grants:` manifest enforcement, E1220) and ParseBlocks.rs manifest validation made coverage-aware too (root-only validation, ancestor-covers matching) rather than left flat-only. Deliberately did NOT retag real Core stdlib call sites (core.fs/jet.db/…) with leaves — first attempt did (Fs.Read/Fs.Write on core.fs read/write, Db.Read/Db.Write on query/execute) and it broke an EXISTING byte-identical snapshot (tests/ui/effect_caps_out_of_set.stderr: `Fs` → `Fs.Read` wording drift) since ancestor-subsumption doesn't change accept/reject there, only the leaf-tagging choice did — reverted. Leaf precision is instead a pure user-declared-contract concept: D-PROP1's existing 'seed a fn's own `direct` set with its declared positive effects' mechanism means `fn load() #(Fs.Read) {...}` publishes `Fs.Read` regardless of body, which is exactly the ballot's own load/archive/boot illustration (no bodies shown) and needed zero changes to any Core effect-production call site — full backward compat, zero wording drift anywhere. Found and fixed one latent bug the new tree case exposed: E0749's message reconstructed `#(!…)` from the *reached* effect set instead of the *declared* prohibited set — invisible pre-D-EFFTREE1 (reached always == declared in the flat world) but wrong once a leaf can be reached under a broader declared root (`#(!Fs)` prohibiting a `Fs.Write` call was rendering `#(!Fs.Write)`); fixed by passing both sets through, verified against the one existing E0749 snapshot (unchanged, reached==declared there too). No new diagnostic code needed — E0119 already covers an unknown root by construction (`parse_effect_name` checks only the root segment), and the ballot's own worked examples confirm leaves are open/unvalidated, not a second closed vocabulary. docs: syntax-decisions.md's D-EFF4/D-EFF5 entry updated in place (flat→tree-root framing) + new D-EFFTREE1 entry added matching the D-TAG1/D-PATCH1/D-FIELDPOL1 entries' terse voice; also fixed an unrelated stale doc reference two lines below (D-EFF3's impl-obligation code was documented as E0710, which was never a real emitted code — the actual code has always been E0742; trivial adjacent fix, confirmed via diagnostics_coverage's registered-code tests). New example examples/features/effects/effect_tree.jet (load/archive/boot, mirrors the ballot's worked example almost verbatim) + golden .out, manually verified via `nix develop -c ./target/debug/jet run` (byte-identical to the .out written) — full golden suite is the orchestrator's job per the testing-discipline instructions, not run here. New tests/ui/effect_tree_sibling_rejected.{jet,stderr} for the new precision-violation case (Fs.Write call under a Fs.Read bound), blessed via UPDATE_EXPECT and read against diagnostics.md's E0740 row before keeping. New fmt STABILITY test (tests/fmt.rs::fmt_preserves_dotted_effect_paths) — formatter needed zero code changes since effect names were always opaque strings end to end, dots pass through every existing emission site untouched; this pins that down. Verified byte-identical (all read, none blessed away): every existing effects-adjacent snapshot (tests/ui/effect_*.stderr, grant_*.stderr, taint_sink_unsanitized.stderr, pure/live/stdin *_e3401/e3403.stderr) via `cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots` (ui_snapshots + lint_snapshots both green); tests/effects.rs (47), tests/taint.rs (12), tests/capabilities.rs (4), tests/capability_determinism.rs (4), tests/web_partition.rs (7) all green unchanged; tests/fmt.rs (86, incl. the new one); tests/diagnostics_coverage.rs (6, confirms no orphaned/unregistered code) and tests/gen_errors.rs. Manually confirmed the three specific ballot behaviors live (not just via unit tests): `#(Fs)` accepts a `Fs.Read`/`Fs.Write` callee (ancestor subsumes descendant); `#(Fs.Read)` rejects a sibling `Fs.Write` callee (E0740, the new precision — this is the new ui snapshot); `#Grant(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` call inside its scope (E0712, D-SCAP1 subtree precision) while a `Fs.Read` call inside the same grant succeeds; `#(!Fs)` prohibits a `Fs.Write` reached transitively (E0749, ancestor-prohibits-descendant, the symmetric reading); depth-3 paths (`Net.Http.Get`) parse and check with no hardcoded depth limit; an unknown root (`Bogus.Read`) is still E0119. `cargo build --workspace` clean, `cargo test --no-run --workspace` clean except one PRE-EXISTING unrelated break (tests/reflect.rs missing `computed` field on AST::Field — not touched by this card, not caused by D-EFFTREE1, left for whoever owns that in-flight work). No git commits made. Card done pending orchestrator's full golden re-verification.

D-EFFTREE1 implementation dispatched to a subagent (last item on this card). Brief covers: dotted effect-path parsing (`Fs.Read`), ancestor-subsumption in Effects.rs/Registration.rs's E0740 check (same rule as D-TAG1's group matching, reused conceptually), D-SCAP1 grant subtree precision, D-PROP1 prohibition symmetry, mandatory regression check of every existing effects-related snapshot/example (this reopens a ratified, shipped, no-subsumption decision — backward compat with all ten flat names is non-negotiable). [handoff] if this session ends before it reports back, check its result before assuming incomplete.

Orchestrator re-verification of D-FIELDPOL1 (never trust a subagent's own green): full `cargo test --test golden` run twice by the orchestrator itself (never delegated to the subagent, corrected an earlier misstep where a subagent burned it). First run failed on an UNRELATED pre-existing bug — examples/features/expected/types/nested_enum_groups.out (D-TAG1's own fixture) had a stray CLI stderr-banner line ("effects: Io", jet build/run's D-EFFBUDGET1 eprintln) baked into the golden stdout fixture; fixed by removing it and confirming the compiled binary's real stdout matches. Second full golden run clean. D-TAG1/D-PATCH1/D-FIELDPOL1 all independently verified done. Next: D-EFFTREE1 (last item).

D-FIELDPOL1 implemented: `name: T => expr` computed struct field, never stored, recomputed on every read. Parser (`=>` after field type), Field.computed: Option<Box<Expr>>. Sema (CheckerFieldPolicy.rs, new): E0338 cycle check over the computed-field dependency graph (self-reference included) via a DFS colored-visit; rewrites sibling bare-idents in the expr to `self.<field>`; synthesizes a `fn <field>(self) -> T { return <expr>; }` method appended to `s.methods` so it flows through the ordinary method-registration/body-check/TIR-codegen pipeline (no new lowering path, mirrors the S62 delegation-method precedent) — TypeRegistry gained a `computed_fields` side table (struct→field→(span,type)) so a computed field is NEVER in the struct-literal required/allowed field list (E0339 if provided) or writable (`s.field=v`/`s.field++`, also E0339), but a *read* still resolves its type. Codegen: computed field excluded from the Rust struct's member list and from `@[Patchable]`'s `T.Patch`/apply/diff/merge (verified the combo works, no new plumbing needed); `Cx.computed_fields` + a `LowerEnv.self_owner` field (self's own env type is `None` by design, so `self.field` needed a different owner-lookup than `x.field`) route every `Expr::Field` read of a computed field — inside the getter itself, inside any other method, and at ordinary call sites — to a getter call instead of a member access; `@[Codable]` encode calls the getter (field appears in the wire), decode skips it. Formatter round-trips `=> expr`; fmt STABILITY test added. Example examples/features/types/computed_field.jet + golden .out. docs/spec/diagnostics.md + syntax-decisions.md updated. Known gaps (named, not silently skipped): the sibling-reference rewrite does not descend into a lambda body or an if-expression's statement block (safe — surfaces as an ordinary sema unknown-name error, never a miscompile, per I2) — only a plain formula expression is covered end-to-end; JetShow (`jet_show`) on a non-generic struct still uses Rust's derived `{:?}` and won't show a computed field (JetDebug does, via the getter, on both generic and non-generic paths); the Cranelift JIT dev-loop tier's separate struct-field lowering (`Codegen::TIR::mod::lower_jit_program`) was not wired for computed fields. All targeted suites green: cargo build --workspace, --test tir (142 passed), --test fmt (84 passed, incl. new fmt_preserves_computed_fields), --test diagnostic_snapshots (ui_snapshots + lint_snapshots), --test diagnostics_coverage (6/6). Next: D-EFFTREE1.

D-PATCH1 hardening: fixed I2 regression from D-TAG1's Eq/Hash enum derive (broke any comparable enum with a non-hashable payload field, e.g. CLI subcommand args, or a Named field that itself had Float — added a proper `hashable` set, fixed-point over Named refs, gated struct+enum derive on it). Fixed Bundle.rs double-firing E0336/E0337 (inject_patchable_types + validate_patchable_items both validated the same structs — dropped the redundant pass). Closed I4 gap: E0336/E0337 now have diagnostics.md rows + tests/ui snapshots (patchable_generic, patchable_stored_ref) + D-PATCH1 logged in syntax-decisions.md. golden/hardening/tir/diagnostic_snapshots/diagnostics_coverage all green. D-FIELDPOL1 implementation now running in a subagent — next after: D-EFFTREE1.

D-PATCH1 vertical slice: `@[Patchable]` → synthetic `T.Patch` (optional fields, partial `.{ }` literals), `apply`/`diff`/`merge` codegen, example patchable.jet. E0336/E0337 for generic/ref/fn fields. Patch Encode/Decode deferred (prelude path). Card building — next: D-FIELDPOL1, D-EFFTREE1.

Owner unfroze; implementation started in parallel with jetpack. Order: D-TAG1 → D-PATCH1 → D-FIELDPOL1 → D-EFFTREE1 (EFFTREE last — reopens E0740). [handoff] D-TAG1 agent running; none spec-logged in syntax-decisions.md yet — each implementation adds its entry.
Activated into epoch e3 track

Owner directive 2026-07-03: parked — none of the four ratified features (D-TAG1/D-PATCH1/D-FIELDPOL1/D-EFFTREE1, all =A) sit on the jetpack critical path, and jetpack is the priority. Frozen with ratifications intact; activate when language-feature work resumes (post-jetpack). Not counted against e3 completion.

4 ballots minted from gameplay-dna.md: D-TAG1, D-PATCH1, D-FIELDPOL1, D-EFFTREE1 (no ID collisions; D-EFFTREE1 is an explicit reopen of ratified D-EFF4/5). Each carries gist/story/inWild/comparisons/options-with-worked-code/rec. Card holds in deciding until owner decides.

Rev 2 after devil's-advocate pass + owner directive (standard-language-feel, no foreign systems). Every transplant now lands as known machinery with a today-vs-proposed comparison per section. Killed: `tag` keyword (collides ratified D-QUAL2 tag qualifier; I8 second enum) -> nested enum variant groups + core Bag<T> instead of TagSet/TagQuery; relative patch magnitudes `+1` and invert() -> @[Patchable] derive with absolute-value T.Patch struct + diff/merge; purge.available() runtime query (arity unsolved) -> tooling-only, section 3 stays zero-ballot; derived-field `= expr` spelling (steals the field-default slot) -> `name: T => expr`. cards.title: Blueprint-class visual editor for Jet (full-fidelity, bidirectional)
cards.body: Owner directive (2026-07-02): a FULLY functional Blueprint-style visual editor for Jet is VERY important, especially since Blueprint will no longer be in UE6 — an open market gap Jet can fill. North-star principles: text is the single source of truth, the graph view is a projection (semantic-index/LSP powered, D-SEMINDEX1); round-trip is lossless (same bar as the formatter STABILITY law); FULL fidelity — every language feature representable in the graph, no 'drop to code' cliff; type-directed pin dragging is the expected-type elaboration the language already builds toward (Blueprint north-star). Dependencies to sequence behind: LSP maturity, semantic index API (D-IMPACT1/D-ASKCODE1 stack), dossier/outline (D-DOSSIER1), structural merge (e7 cards — graph diffs need semantic merge), formatter round-trip guarantees. First planning deliverable: architecture doc (projection model, edit protocol, persistence = plain .jet files) + decision list for owner-facing surface (node taxonomy, where the editor lives: LSP client vs standalone vs web).

cards.title: Runtime schema-migration engine (make decode actually apply migration{} blocks)
cards.body: Surfaced by #105: D-MIGRATE1/2 ship compile-time intent checks (E0910) only — codegen erases migration{} blocks, so old-shaped stored data fails decode instead of migrating, and decode_traced (D-MIGRATE3=A) can never report migrated=true. log.text: Implemented + verified; full suite green; committed. cards.title: v5 companion syntax decrees (owner-ratified 2026-07-03)
cards.body: Six owner decrees issued during memory-model v5 review; ratified directly, no ballot needed. Greenfield rule: pre-release spellings leave zero trace — old forms are simply not part of the grammar/stdlib and fail as ordinary unknown syntax; no diagnostics reference them. GREENFIELD RULE (owner 2026-07-03): pre-release spellings leave zero trace — no compat shims, no diagnostics mentioning former forms; old spellings simply are not in the grammar/stdlib and fail as ordinary unknown syntax. (1) D-EMPTYLIT1: empty collection literal is [] for list/map/set alike, type-directed; [:] is not part of the grammar. (2) D-OPT-SPELL1: option constructors are Val(x) / None; value(x) and null do not exist; pattern tests are `== Val(n)`. (3) D-LAMBDA-INFER1: bare lambda params legal wherever the type is inferable (m => m.hp > 0); typed form stays for ambiguity. (4) D-TUPLE-DESTRUCT1: tuple-destructuring binding (a, b) := f(); tasks.channel() returns (Sender<T>, Receiver<T>). (5) D-FILES-WRITE1: core.files is THE file module (no core.fs; users may alias); handle method is .write. (6) D-STR-AFTER1: String gains .after(sep) (+ .before family, exact set minted at impl). Implementation: parser/sema/stdlib + examples + fmt round-trip + ui/golden snapshots + syntax-decisions.md rows + Syntax.rs I7 entries where new tokens. Independent of D-MEM1 sequencing.
